(Google Maps) A Lake Country woman recently pleaded guilty to animal cruelty charges after she attempted to euthanize her cat using fentanyl. On May 29, Jayme-Jo Crystal Brooks pleaded guilty in Kelowna court for "administering a poisonous or injurious drug or substance to a domestic animal. " On Christmas Day 2024, Brooks was investigated by the BC SPCA after the attempt to euthanize one of her three cats by injecting it with fentanyl. A veterinarian called the BC SPCA helpline, reporting a cat in distress. It's unknown how the veterinarian found the cat after Brooks' euthanization attempt. The SPCA ordered a necropsy, which revealed the fentanyl exposure. After this discovery, the SPCA executed a search warrant of Brooks' residence, where two other cats were found and seized. Upon investigation, the cats were found to have cocaine, amphetamines, and methamphetamine in their systems. One of the cats was safe and adopted by a "loving family. " The other suffered too many underlying health concerns and was humanely euthanized upon the recommendation of veterinarians. The SPCA called Brooks' conviction "victorious. " "This is a huge victory for animal welfare in Canada, " said Jamie Wiltse, regional manager of animal protection services. "We often see charges go through at the provincial level under the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (PCA) Act, but this case was prosecuted under the Criminal Code of Canada. "A criminal code conviction sends a stronger message and reflects a higher level of societal condemnation and accountability, and is typically reserved for the most serious cases. Unlike a provincial offence conviction, a conviction under the criminal code carries the consequence of a criminal record. " In response to her guilty plea, Brooks received a five-year prohibition of owning, having the custody or control of or residing in the same premises as an animal or a bird. She is also on a one-year probation order with "several" conditions in place, which include her to engage in counselling or education programs as directed by a probation officer and ordered to complete 30 hours of community service work. In 2025, the BC SPCA conducted more than 7, 600 animal cruelty investigations.

A Winnipeg pharmacist who left unlabelled prescription drugs in an unmarked bag for pickup with an employee at a fast-food restaurant has been disciplined for professional misconduct. One of the medications was in the narcotic category, according to a decision recently released by the College of Pharmacists of Manitoba. An investigator with the regulatory body for pharmacists found the case revealed issues with narcotic accountability and with dispensing frequent and high doses of opioids. Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement The case goes back to 2019, when the college received a police report about the pharmacist leaving the unlabelled drugs at a Dairy Queen restaurant. The pharmacist had been contacted by a patient who had pain and fever following dental surgery, says the decision by a College of Pharmacists discipline committee. A nurse practitioner had prescribed the patient naproxen (an anti-inflammatory sold under brand names like Aleve), clindamycin (an antibiotic) and Tylenol No. 3 with codeine, which is classified as a narcotic, the decision says. The prescription was faxed to the pharmacy, which was closed at the time, but the pharmacist drove there and prepared medications for the patient. Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement The pharmacist took the unlabelled drugs in an unmarked bag to a nearby Dairy Queen and handed it to "a young employee" of the restaurant, the decision says. "She did not confirm the name of the DQ staff member nor did she make any attempt to confirm that the staff member was familiar with the patient, " according to the decision. The pharmacist then sent a text to someone - whose name is redacted in the report - saying "meds done and delivered. " It's not clear from the decision why the pharmacist took the medications to the restaurant, as opposed to another location. Escorted back to pharmacy by police A person, whose name is redacted, arrived to pick up the prescription, but the Dairy Queen owners refused to release the medications, the decision says. Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Police were then contacted and arrived at the restaurant. The pharmacist also returned there, after which police escorted her back to the pharmacy. She attached prescription labels to the medication bottles, which police then delivered, the decision says. It says the panel found the pharmacist's actions contravened the requirement under Canada's Narcotic Control Regulations to ensure that all drugs "are secured against theft, loss or diversion. " The regulations also require that if a drug is a narcotic, the packaging must have a warning sticker, and the patient must be given an information handout specific to the narcotic being sold, the decision says. A spokesperson for the College of Pharmacists of Manitoba said the discipline panel ordered that its decision be made public because it 'serves to protect the public and uphold transparency and trust in the pharmacy profession. ' (Tyson KoschikCBC) After the incident, the pharmacist voluntarily surrendered her licence to practise and resigned as manager of the pharmacy. Her licence was reinstated by the college's complaints committee in September 2020. Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement However, the decision says the pharmacist was "found to be practising as a pharmacist in the dispensary at the pharmacy" while her licence was voluntarily surrendered. That resulted in an additional disciplinary charge. A hearing into disciplinary charges against the pharmacist was held in December 2023, where she entered guilty pleas to multiple counts under the Pharmaceutical Act. The complaints committee entered a stay for some of the counts. The pharmacist was ordered to pay 150, 000 in penalties, including a fine of 20, 000 and 130, 000 toward the costs of the investigation and hearing. She was given a one-year suspension from practice, but was given credit for 10 months of the time during which she had voluntarily surrendered her licence. Sorry for mistake: pharmacist The discipline panel issued its decision in March 2024, but the pharmacist then filed an appeal at the Manitoba Court of Appeal. Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement The appeal was discontinued in April 2025, and the regulatory body published the case on its website a few weeks later. Neely Hammerberg, a communications co-ordinator for the pharmacists' college, said in a statement to CBC the discipline panel issued an order "to publish and make available to the public the decision, which serves to protect the public and uphold transparency and trust in the pharmacy profession. " CBC also contacted the pharmacist after the decision was released. "I'm sorry for making the mistake, " she said, adding that she's working with the college on the guidelines she's been given. Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement "All I wanted was what is best for my patient, " she said. "My patients are still my priority, and their care is still my priority, and I'll continue working towards fixing my practices. " In addition to the Dairy Queen incident, the college's investigation also found the pharmacy where the pharmacist worked had a counselling room for patients, which was described as having prescription files stacked nearly to the ceiling. Using that room for patient consultations "put the confidentiality of patient information at risk, " because the labels of prescription bags contained confidential health information, the decision said. The counselling room also had a large narcotic safe, which was left unlocked and open, according to the decision. Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Anyone coming in through the building's back door "had a view of the interior of the narcotic safe, with nothing to stop them from accessing narcotic storage, " it says. The investigation also found that the pharmacy didn't keep accurate counts of drugs in its inventory of narcotic and controlled substances. Narcotic counts completed at the pharmacy "revealed that there were significant unexplained drug shortages, " the decision says. It also says the pharmacy dispensed a lot of opioid prescriptions for many patients, with some at very high doses. The pharmacist had no documentation to show she had been working with prescribers to lower patients' high doses of opioids, and admitted she didn't meet her professional obligations on that, the decision says. Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement The March 2024 decision notes the pharmacist had previously been disciplined, while practising as a pharmacist in British Columbia. In 2012, the College of Pharmacists of British Columbia found she had prepared "a fraudulent employment document under the letterhead and purported signature of her current employer, " which she then submitted to a prospective employer. She was given a 30-day licence suspension and fined 3, 000.

The 900 block of Victoria's Pandora Avenue is often referred to as the epicentre of the city's opioid crisis. (Olivier LaurinVictoria News) While politics, sports, the housing crisis and rising cost of living all made headlines more than once this year, homelessness, drug use and mental health have also been under the spotlight. As 2025 comes to a close, Victoria News spoke with the CEOs of Our Place Society and Pacifica Housing about the past year and what lies ahead in 2026. While the previous 12 months brought successes, both organizations were transparent about the challenges they also faced. "We spent most of this year feeling quite hopeless at times, " said Our Place's Julian Daly. "We've seen entrenched encampments and people who are utterly unhoused - maybe even 'unhousable' - on our streets suffering from mental illness and deep drug addiction. "To witness that every day and to see it not changing in any positive way has been very difficult. " Julian Daly, CEO of Our Place Society. (Olivier LaurinVictoria News) However, an increased police presence on Pandora Avenue and in the downtown core, under Victoria's newly launched Community Safety and Wellbeing Plan, has helped reduce tensions, Daly said. The initiative, aimed at addressing complex issues linked to homelessness and public drug use, has already led to what Daly described as a "significant reduction" in street camping, along with a stronger sense of security around the 900 block of Pandora. He added that enforcement of this plan also weakened what he called a "culture of impunity, " which has "receded with daily power washing and bylaw enforcement on Pandora, " as officers began issuing charges for open drug use. "This has been really helpful in terms of deterring some of the people who have been on Pandora exploiting the unhoused folks, " he said, adding the measures have also discouraged drug dealers from frequenting the area. "It made Pandora feel safer, and it certainly allowed a lot of people - who maybe were a bit frightened - to come into our buildings, especially for our meal services. " Yet despite the progress made and new hopes building up in the community, a major challenge remains, said Daly. "People who are currently unhoused are essentially 'unhousable' because of their addictions and mental health challenges, " he said. "Until their needs are addressed, nothing will change for them. It's really as simple as that. "Housing first is great for people who are ready for housing, but for those who are not ready because of their conditions, they need health first. " Both Our Place Society and Pacifica Housing's outreach teams witnessed this recurring trend firsthand while working on the streets of downtown Victoria and the surrounding areas. Carolina Ibarra, CEO of Pacifica Housing - one of the largest providers of housing and support services on Vancouver Island - said that while overall numbers of folks in the streets are down, her team still encounters about 35 to 40 people sleeping in doorways. Pacifica Housing CEO Carolina Ibarra (left) and Lisa Feeney, manager of community services, at the organization's downtown office. (Olivier LaurinVictoria News) While both CEOs agree that the challenges they face are largely similar, their approaches to addressing them differ. For Ibarra, supportive housing, which combines affordable rents with on-site support services, is what's urgently missing. "A lot of people that we're seeing out there very specifically need supportive housing, " she said. While Pacifica already offers housing for over 1, 500 residents, the needs remain. "Our number one barrier is just not having sufficiently well-staffed, purpose-built, supportive housing, " she said. "Where we sit now, there's a lot of uncertainty because we keep hearing that there's no money. " Amid dwindling funds, in part caused by the ongoing U. S. -Canada trade war and increasing austerity measures under the Eby government, resources have become increasingly tight this year, Ibarra explained. Although the provincial government currently funds many supportive housing facilities across B. C. , these efforts often fall short of making a substantial impact when funding is insufficient. "A lot of the supportive housing sites have very light support, " said Ibarra. "Most of the sites, not just including ours, have less than half the staff (they need). " "Quite bluntly, we don't have the services to support the people on Pandora, so that does need to happen because many of those folks may not be ready to go to recovery. They need to stabilize first, and then they can go to recovery to move on. " In the new year, Ibarra hopes the federal government will step up and fund the building of new facilities, while the province continues supporting existing service providers. A concerted effort by all community stakeholders and levels of government is needed, according to Ibarra, to achieve a permanent solution rather than temporary, lower-cost fixes. "I'm hoping that the province will realize that there is no way to not pay for the housing crisis, " she said. "You either invest and pay for solutions, or you're gonna pay even more in homelessness management. "We just need to commit and invest. " In parallel, Daly is also seeking continued government funding for additional treatment and second-stage housing. "What we need is more of what's working, and this includes detox beds, " he said. "We've basically had the same number of detox beds in Victoria - which is about 22 - for the last six years. Yet we've seen an increase in people who potentially need it. "I'd also love to see more treatment and recovery beds (as well as) involuntary care beds. . . for people who are most unwell. " Despite this year's numerous trials and tribulations, both CEOs said 2025 also contained its successes. For Our Place, one of the year's main highlights was the continued success of New Road, the organization's recovery centre located in View Royal, which offers 40 beds for men and 20 new spaces for women. "What stood out for me, as an organization, is our continued work of moving folk from barely surviving to thriving; moving folk off the street, into housing and into treatment, " he said. With a graduation rate of 73 per cent, Daly explained the program helped hundreds of people break free from addiction, maintain sobriety and return to an active role in the community. Daly added that another high point was the launch of Our Place's landscaping company, Your Place, which employs up to 20 people who have completed New Road's program. For Ibarra, the year's highlight was expanding the organization's housing stock with The Fern - a new, purpose-built 88-unit affordable rental development in Victoria. This addition, part of a regional push by the province and local housing providers, helped deliver 500 new homes for low-income residents across the South Island in 2025. The influx of new units led to a slight drop in rental prices, a development welcomed by the community. Looking at 2026, Ibarra and Daly are under no illusions about the "uncertainties" and "worrisome trends" ahead, mainly around funding. Still, both are optimistic about the progress that can be made. Although "a lot of work still needs to be done, there is reason for hope, " concluded Daly. "We can still see those challenges, " said Ibarra, "But we really have come so far. For organizations like mine, it is important to recognize the really important work that has been done. The challenges that remain don't take away from that progress. "

An influencer from Ecuador stood at Yonge and Dundas Square last week and gave Toronto zero stars. "This is downtown, " he said. "This is the flagship of Toronto. And there's literally garbage, crackheads, crazy people, people talking to themselves. " The panel on Friday's Rebel Roundtable livestream said he wasn't wrong. The panel discussion opened with a different clip, one featuring a tourist in Vancouver whose bags were stolen from a hotel lobby by two opportunistic drug users who then drained 600 from his bank account. Drea Humphrey, a B. C. resident, noted that Vancouver has 60 more property crime than Los Angeles. "It's an absolute embarrassment, " she said, particularly given the hundreds of millions spent on hosting FIFA's World Cup. Independent journalist Elie Cantin-Nantel has been flying across the country since January documenting its decline, and detailed how between 2014 and 2024, Toronto saw a 160 increase in shootings, a 47 increase in homicides, a 53 increase in assaults, and an 86 increase in car thefts. Homelessness is up 110 in three years. "Our country is in decline, " he said. "It is in decline. " He pointed to Japan - where strict criminal laws and functioning mental health institutions mean a Louis Vuitton store operates inside the main train station. "Can you imagine a designer store at Union? " he said. "It would get robbed all the time. " Fellow independent journalist Natasha Graham, who reports from Montreal, said she visited Toronto last summer in tourist mode for the first time in years and was shocked. "It is decrepit, " she said. "The infrastructure is falling apart. " She described being physically jostled at the aquarium and seeing a woman foraging through garbage at a suburban mall the night before the show. "I don't think I need to look at people foraging in the garbage in a civilized society, " she said. "I think having someone foraging through the garbage and accepting that - that is a lack of compassion. " David Menzies recalled asking a security guard at Yonge and Dundas Square why the small fountains in the square were shut off at night. The answer: homeless were using them as bidets. "When that is the status quo and authorities know about it and do nothing except shut off the water, " he said, "we have a problem that's not being addressed. " He noted Toronto once had the nickname Toronto the Good. "That ship has sailed, " he said. The panel also reacted to FIFA Vancouver's official World Cup tourism website, which includes a guide on how to consume illegal drugs - advising visitors to "start slow" and use "one substance at a time. " Drea called it "so embarrassing. " Elie said FIFA should be telling visitors these drugs are illegal and carry criminal consequences, not publishing a how-to guide. "I guarantee you in Qatar they weren't telling people how to use drugs, " he said. "It is not normal that people from the third world say their third world countries feel safer than Canada, " Elie said. "We cannot allow this to continue being normalized. " Rebel Roundtable livestreams air Fridays at 11 a. m. MT 1 p. m. ET on YouTube and Rumble.

Gerid James Gregory-Allen plead guilty on Thursday, April 30, for his role in a drugs and weapons bust in late 2024 outside an overdose prevention site in Nanaimo. (Image Credit: Submitted photo) Federal Crown prosecutor Chris Gibson outlined facts of the case, in which a civilian filed a complaint with the Nanaimo RCMP regarding two individuals who turned out to be Gregory-Allen and Koshman in a vehicle on Cavan St. Gregory-Allen was counting pills, put them in a backpack, and left. Pictures of the pair were sent to Mounties, who were recognized by police investigators. Knowing the pair frequented the Overdose Prevention Site (OPS) at 250 Albert St. , police showed up to investigate. Gregory-Allen was spotted by police with the same backpack pictured by the civilian witness in the front courtyard area of the OPS. Both suspects were arrested on site. Gregory-Allen's backpack contained about 225 grams of methamphetamine, 80 grams of crack cocaine, over 40 grams of fentanyl, bear spray, phones, a scale, and a key to the Castaway Motel on Terminal Ave. He also had a collapsible baton, brass knuckles, a knife, and about 640 cash. Koshman's backpack contained just over seven grams of crack cocaine, 1. 5 grams of fentanyl, opioid pills, brass knuckles, bear spray, drug pipes, and 320 cash. Significant to the investigation was a loaded 3D printed firearm also found in Koshman's backpack; however, the weapon with five bullets belonged to Gregory-Allen. Koshman was adamant the weapon was not hers, with Gregory-Allen taking responsibility for the gun. While the weapon was considered loaded, which was reflected in the charge Gregory-Allen pleaded guilty to on Thursday, the federal Crown's Gibson said the weapon wasn't considered "immediately fireable. " The Crown's Gibson said police secured Gregory-Allen's motel room and obtained a search warrant. "Significantly, there was a loaded sawed-off, break-action shotgun and a pump-action shotgun, which was unloaded but had shells available to be used. There was 10, 000 cash and over a kilogram of different types of drugs: fentanyl, methamphetamine, cocaine, and GHB. " Gibson said a joint submission has been agreed upon with Gregory-Allen's lawyer, amounting to a 10-year prison sentence. Gregory-Allen also pleaded guilty to a pair of drug trafficking charges for an incident on May 2, 2024, outside a supportive housing and resource centre on Wesley St. He was found with 35 grams of crack cocaine and 22 grams of a fentanylcarfentanil mix. Pre-sentence and Gladue reports were issued for Gregory-Allen, who entered guilty pleas from the Nanaimo Correctional Centre. He'll be formally sentenced at a yet-to-be-determined future date. Gregory-Allen has been in custody since the Sept. 12, 2024, offence date. Koshman, who has no prior criminal record, attended the proceedings from a Lower Mainland treatment centre. Court was told Koshman is contesting her sentencing process, and is said to be seeking a non-custodial sentence. News of the bust heightened community tensions around the service, with the executive director of the Canadian Mental Health Association's mid-Island branch pledging a full review of its procedures. Jason Harrison told NanaimoNewsNOW, approximately three weeks after the incident, they're cooperating fully with a police investigation. "Should any gaps or areas for improvement be identified in their internal review, we are fully committed to adopting the necessary changes to strengthen our processes. " Mayor Leonard Krog echoed concerns from those living near the facility and said in October he was "deeply disturbed" by news of the bust. "If these places are to be successful, people have to have confidence in how they are managed, and this certainly, I think, has raised some serious questions that are disturbing, and I hope there will be answers forthcoming, " Krog said. Nanaimo City Council has no jurisdiction over the property or the operator, which falls under a ministerial order formalized in 2016 in response to the ongoing toxic drug crisis. Aaron Manson was entering his fifth and final year of a Bachelor of Business Administration degree at TRU but tragically passed away in 2021 due to an accidental overdose. (Image Credit: Troylana Manson) Aaron Manson 'Be Brave' Gathering at TRU aims to raise awareness about addiction, mental health and the toxic drug crisis Mar 19, 2026 8: 05 AM KAMLOOPS - Kamloops residents are invited to a gathering dedicated to raising awareness about addiction, mental health and the toxic drug crisis. The Aaron Manson "Be Brave" event runs Thursday (March 19) from 6: 30 p. m. to 8: 00 p. m. from the Panorama Room at the International Building on Thompson Rivers University's (TRU) Kamloops campus. TRU says the event honours the memory of the late Aaron Manson. The 26-year-old was entering his fifth and final year of a Bachelor of Business Administration degree at TRU but tragically passed away in 2021 due to an accidental overdose. "Aaron's story is a powerful reminder of the importance of compassion, care and collective responsibility in how we respond to mental health, substance use and loss. We come together each year not only to remember Aaron, but to learn, connect and commit to doing better - together, " TRU states.

Three men arrested in a vehicle theft investigation in Guelph could be connected to similar thefts across southern Ontario. Police said the investigation began on New Year's Eve outside a local gym. Investigators say a Brampton man signed up for a gym membership at the location on Eramosa Road, using a fake name. He then reportedly stole a wallet and keys to a 2017 Toyota Camry from a changeroom, and with the help of another suspect, found the car in the parking lot and drove away in it. "The Guelph Police Service Break Enter Auto Theft Unit took over the investigation and identified a suspect. Officers attended his address in Brampton last Friday (January 9) and located the stolen Camry with a fake licence plate attached, " said police. "While conducting surveillance, officers saw three men, including their suspect, driving in a Toyota van which had been stolen from Toronto earlier that morning. " All three men, from Brampton, were arrested and charged. They range in age from 27 to 32 years old. The investigation is ongoing with police services from other jurisdictions now involved.

Support for Alberta's governing United Conservative Party has increased since October 2025, while a majority of Albertans continue to say the province is on the wrong track, according to Leger's January 2026 Alberta report card. If a provincial election were held today, the UCP would receive 50 per cent of the vote among decided voters, compared with 37 per cent for the Alberta NDP. Support for the governing party is up six percentage points since October 2025, halting a downward trend that began at the start of 2025. Among decided voters, the Alberta Party registered four per cent support. The Republican Party of Alberta, the Alberta Liberal Party and the Solidarity Movement of Alberta each registered two per cent, while the Wildrose Loyalty Coalition, the Green Party of Alberta and "Other" each registered one per cent. Despite the increase in UCP support, 59 per cent of Albertans say the province is on the wrong track, compared with 34 per cent who say it is headed in the right direction. Those results are consistent with findings from October 2025. Views on the province's direction differ by gender and political affiliation. Forty-one per cent of men say Alberta is headed in the right direction, compared with 27 per cent of women. By provincial vote intention, 61 per cent of UCP voters say Alberta is headed in the right direction, compared with 10 per cent of NDP voters. Views on Alberta's place in Canada and separatism A majority of Albertans say the province should remain part of Canada. The survey found 71 per cent of respondents believe Alberta should remain part of Canada, while 18 per cent say it should become an independent country. Five per cent said Alberta should join the United States, and six per cent said they were unsure. Concern about separatist movements is widespread. Fifty-eight per cent of respondents said they are somewhat or very concerned about separatist movements gaining influence in Alberta, compared with 37 per cent who said they are not concerned. Views differ by political affiliation. Among NDP voters, 96 per cent said Alberta should remain part of Canada. Among UCP voters, 52 per cent said Alberta should remain in Canada, while 31 per cent said Alberta should become an independent country. Health care ranks as top issue Health care was the most frequently identified issue facing the province. More than one-quarter of respondents (27 per cent) identified health care as the most important issue facing Alberta, up from 17 per cent in October 2025. Provincial nationalism or separatism ranked second at 11 per cent, an increase of four percentage points over the same period. When first and second most important issues are combined, 43 per cent of respondents cited health care, followed by inflation and rising interest rates (20 per cent), the economy (18 per cent), provincial nationalism or separatism (18 per cent), and housing prices or affordability (15 per cent). Albertans are divided on confidence in accessing health care. Forty-eight per cent said they are confident they and their family will be able to access the care they need when required, while 49 per cent said they are not confident. Confidence varies by gender and political affiliation. Fifty-three per cent of men reported confidence in accessing care, compared with 42 per cent of women. Among UCP voters, 65 per cent said they are confident, compared with 29 per cent of NDP voters. On health care specifically, 24 per cent of respondents said the provincial government has done a good job, while 67 per cent said it has done a bad job. Government approval varies by issue Albertans' assessments of the provincial government vary by policy area. Approval ratings increased since October 2025 in several areas, including energy and pipelines (50 per cent approve), response to wildfire evacuations (48 per cent) and taxes (36 per cent). Approval ratings were lowest for homelessness (21 per cent approve), poverty (23 per cent), housing prices or affordability (23 per cent), the health-care system (24 per cent) and the opioid or drug overdose or toxicity crisis (25 per cent). In each of those areas, a majority of respondents expressed disapproval. Methodology The Leger survey was conducted online among 1, 003 Alberta residents aged 18 and older between Jan. 23 and 26, 2026, using Leger Opinion's online panel. Results were weighted by age, gender, region and education to reflect Alberta's population. Because the survey was conducted using a non-probability panel, a margin of error cannot be formally assigned. For comparison, a probability sample of the same size would have a margin of error of approximately 3. 1 percentage points, 19 times out of 20. Leger noted that its October 2025 wave surveyed eligible voters only and advised caution when interpreting wave-over-wave comparisons.

The B. C. Conservatives have hosted another town hall regarding community safety in the midst of the province's toxic drug crisis. Wednesday, March 18, was the fourth of such town halls that have been hosted in Kelowna in 2026. Politicians from the City of Kelowna, B. C. Conservatives and the federal Conservatives have all taken the opportunity to reassure the public that they are listening and working to fix a public safety crisis threatening businesses and communities. This time around, Kelowna-Mission MLA Gavin Dew headed to Rutland, an area he said is particularly challenged by a rise in homelessness, open drug use and property crime. Dew had recently spoken about Rutland in the legislature. On March 9, he told members of the Legislative Assembly that Rutland businesses are dealing with theft and vandalism due to repeat offenders. He also spoke about Roxanne, a Rutland resident who he said has had to administer naloxone - an opioid overdose countermeasure - more than 50 times. He continued saying she has had people staying on her property using illicit drugs that she has had to kick out. In his Rutland townhall, Dew said his role as government opposition was to hear suggestions by residents and their stories that he can take to the Legislative Assembly to shed a light on the situation in Rutland, hoping to spark change from the B. C. government. More than 150 people attended Wednesday night's town hall. Dew said he's worried about Rutland, likening the drug use situation to an early version of Vancouver's Downtown Eastside neighbourhood. "The downtown eastside in Vancouver, where I used to live, is the most obvious area where that happened, in part because of the concentration of (social) services. What had happened was people ended up clustered there, and a feedback loop persisted in part because there was a concentration of (social) services, a concentration of individuals, a concentration of drug dealers and a concentration of businesses, " he said. "What I see some of what's happening in Rutland is that concentration of (social) services, that concentration of population creates a feedback loop that's not a good thing. " One woman at the town hall, also concerned with public safety in Rutland, argued the opposite. She said Rutland actually has a lack of social services, causing those experiencing homelessness to start fires to avoid the cold weather. "By not having any basic services, we are turning Rutland into a giant bonfire, " she said. Another resident who lives in a seniors' building said the women in his building don't feel safe walking around the neighbourhood anymore because of the drug paraphernalia left out on the streets. A Rutland woman living near the Ministry of Social Development building on Dougall Road and Highway 33 said the building's opening in 2023 has brought more open drug use to the area. She said the government handled the opening of the building poorly, not consulting with the neighbourhood before it opened. Dew, remembering the instance, backed up her claims, saying he urged the province to communicate with the community before its opening and that they didn't listen to his advice. Another Rutland resident said they understood that the change in provincial policy surrounding drug use and mandatory care will take time. In the interim, they called for further safety patrols. Currently, Kelowna bylaw officers conduct foot patrols in Rutland on Tuesdays and Thursdays, according to information from Community Safety Director Darren Caul. The City of Kelowna had also recently mentioned that public disorder-related RCMP calls are up 27 per cent from last year so far. During the town hall, Dew was firm in taking the policy stances of many of his Conservative colleagues, as well as Kelowna Mayor Tom Dyas. Dew highlighted two areas for change in the provincial government regarding public safety. He said he was in favour of more crown prosecutors to lessen the backlog of pending charges to stop repeat offenders. Additionally, Dew spoke in favour of mandatory compassionate care for people entrenched in illicit drug use, adding that more drug users are being afflicted with brain damage as a result of being revived from overdose.

Durham police are concerned there could be more victims after an Oshawa man was arrested for sexual assault, child sexual abuse and more. They say the victim contacted a man and woman with several children in 2025 via a Facebook au pair group to come to Canada to work informally as au pair. In December of 2025, the woman arrived in Canada from Europe and lived with the suspect and his spouse in exchange for providing child care. On December 12, the suspect gave the victim ice cream and soon after eating it, she felt incoherent and went unconscious with no recollection of the night. She then sought medical attention and it was confirmed a noxious drug was present in her system. In early 2026, officers carried out a search warrant at the man's Oshawa home and found several electronic devices and the same drug found in the au pair's system. Investigators found further evidence to support their investigation on the devices including evidence of child sexual abuse and exploitation materials. On Wednesday, June 10, 2026, investigators with the Special Victims Unit took the suspect into custody without incident. Derek Stephen Bellamy, 38, from Oshawa is charged with sexual assault, administer noxious substance, voyeurism x5, possess recording obtained by voyeurism x5, possess child sexual abuse and exploitation material, access child sexual abuse and exploitation material. TORONTO - Canada Border Services Agency says a drug smuggling investigation has led to the arrests of two suspects who allegedly used online advertisements to recruit women to smuggle cannabis out of Toronto Pearson International Airport. It says the nine-month investigation, carried out jointly with the RCMP, began after two Canadian women were detained in Nigeria while trying to bring cannabis into the country. The RCMP and CBSA allege both women were recruited through an advertisement on "LeoList, " a classifieds website, with an offer of up to 20, 000 for transporting illegal drugs while travelling overseas out of Pearson Airport. They say officers intercepted an additional shipment of 29 kilograms of cannabis before it left Canada. The suspects, one from Toronto and the other from the United Kingdom, are facing multiple drug smuggling-related charges. The CBSA says the accused men were released on bail and will appear in court on Jan. 16. This report by The Canadian Press was first published Dec. 22, 2025. The Canadian Press

Frank GunnThe Canadian Press At least five cutting-edge clinical trials for childhood cancer have been closed to new Canadian patients because of the Trump administration's cuts to scientific funding and its directive that grants no longer be shared with foreign researchers. Toronto's Hospital for Sick Children halted enrolment in three trials for incurable brain cancer last month after the U. S. National Cancer Institute decided not to renew funding for a consortium of pediatric brain-tumour scientists whose only Canadian site was at SickKids. The three trials were testing novel treatments for children with rare and deadly brain tumours, including a cancer-fighting vaccine and CAR-T therapy, a type of immunotherapy in which patients' own white blood cells are genetically engineered to attack their cancer. "How frustrating would it be to be a parent who knew that there was a treatment somewhere that could save their child, and not be able to access it because it's not available in Canada? " said Jim Whitlock, the division head of hematology and oncology at SickKids. Part of the Pediatric Brain Tumor Consortium's research may be moved to another early-phase trial network in the United States, but that network closed its studies to international researchers in July, leading two other clinical trials to stop enrolling Canadian patients. One of those trials was geared to cancer in infants. The Trump administration's sweeping cuts to the National Institutes of Health and its vow to end sub-grants to foreign researchers are hitting pediatric-cancer research in Canada particularly hard - even though the dollar amounts involved are relatively small. Opinion: Trump might come after our drug prices. Universities need to help us play defence That's because the latest experimental treatments for childhood cancer, which is rare to begin with, are targeted at ever-narrower subtypes of tumours. Canadian scientists have to co-operate with U. S. and international researchers to enroll enough children to make a go of such precision medicines studies. "It's like looking for that needle in the haystack, " said Kathy Brodeur-Robb, the executive director of C17 Council, a research network made up of Canada's pediatric oncology programs. "You need to be finding these kids from all over the place to try and test theories. Otherwise, you're going to have studies open for 15 years, and that's not going to help any child with cancer. " Ms. Brodeur-Robb said the past few weeks have been "chaos" as the Canadian pediatric-cancer community deals with the fallout of U. S. funding cuts and policy shifts. Dr. Whitlock added that the situation underscores how much Canada has come to depend on American government money and leadership in international medical research. "Just as Canada has made a decision that we need to be more self-reliant and invest in submarines and fighter planes and Arctic radar, I think the question on the table is, is Canada going to be self-sufficient in ensuring that its children have access to the best available cancer treatments? " South of the border, the Pediatric Brain Tumor Consortium learned through an Aug. 19 memo titled "Difficult news regarding PBTC funding" that its grant of about US4-million annually would expire next March, after which it would "cease to exist. " Shribman: Trump and Kennedy are the modern-day Odd Couple The consortium decided a few days later to pause new enrolments for six clinical trials, including the three with participants at SickKids, said neuro-oncologist Vijay Ramaswamy, principal investigator for the consortium's SickKids site. "The suddenness, I think, is what hit all of us, " Dr. Ramaswamy said. He said the SickKids site received less than 100, 000 annually from the consortium, an amount determined by the number of patients the Toronto hospital enrolled in PBTC studies. There are six Canadian children from across the country enrolled in the CAR-T trial for brain cancer. Another three are enrolled in the study of a vaccine for brain tumours. They'll stay in the trials and continue to be monitored, Dr. Ramaswamy said. But other Canadian children can no longer join the trials. Three other brain-cancer trials that SickKids was preparing to open this year have been paused. A second PBTC memo that Dr. Ramaswamy shared with The Globe and Mail suggests that some of the consortium's work could be moved under the umbrella of another group funded by the U. S. National Cancer Institute, which is part of the NIH. But that group, the Pediatric Early Phase-Clinical Trial Network (PEP-CTN), closed its trials to international sites as of July 31, according to Thai Tran, a pediatric oncologist at CHU Sainte-Justine, a children's hospital in Montreal. Dr. Tran is the medical director in Canada for PEP-CTN and the Children's Oncology Group, another research network funded through the NIH. He's been told by his U. S. counterparts that PEP-CTN studies are no longer open to Canadian or international participants. "So even if we can actually find a way to fund those trials, " Dr. Tran said, "we would not be able to participate at this moment. " Over all, the U. S. National Cancer Institute, through its Children's Oncology Group, gave a total of US1. 2-million in funding to Canadian research sites last year, Ms. Brodeur-Robb of C17 said. In an emailed statement on Friday, the NIH said it will support international scientific collaboration with foreign scientists and researchers "when conducted in a secure, justifiable, and responsible way. " "NIH takes very seriously proper stewardship of federal funds as well as any issues related to maintaining national security. We must know when American taxpayer money is supporting foreign institutions or personnel, " it said. Editor's note: This story on published on Thursday, Sept. 11 and updated Friday, Sept. 12 with comment from the U. S. National Institutes of Health

VANCOUVER - One of the founders of a "compassion club" that sold safety-tested heroin, cocaine and other drugs told a B. C. Supreme Court constitutional challenge that they felt "invincible" and hoped media coverage of their operation would spur public conversation. But Jeremy Kalicum of the Drug User Liberation Front says he now believes the publicity led to their arrests. He told the court in Vancouver that he and co-founder Eris Nyx were uncomfortable engaging with the media, but coverage of the club's operations added to public knowledge and aligned with the club's principles of transparency and accountability. Kalicum and Nyx were found guilty this month on charges of possession of drugs for the purpose of trafficking, but their conviction is on hold until the constitutional challenge has been decided. Kalicum told the court under cross-examination by Crown lawyer Oren Bick that they knew the club was controversial, with government involvement putting them in the public eye, and a harsh public backlash and political pressure led to their closure in October 2023. The court heard earlier that the group had been funded by the Vancouver Coastal Health Authority to test illicit street drugs, but DULF went further by buying and testing drugs to distribute in order to prevent further overdoses. Kalicum said no drugs were bought with health authority money, drug purchases were financed by donations, and sales were made at cost to club members. He said he now believes engaging with the media and putting the club in the public eye is what led to their arrests, and he feels that they were "thrown under the bus by multiple institutions. " Bick questioned Kalicum about the data and research they were producing and conducting on more than three dozen club members who accessed the club's drugs and site, and Kalicum says they published information about the club to be transparent about their work. A post to DULF's website, dated March 3, 2025, says its legal challenge is seeking to prove that a section of the Controlled Drugs and Substances Act that prohibits possession of drugs for the purpose of trafficking is unconstitutional and "its enforcement is killing the very people it purports to protect. " This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 26, 2025. Darryl Greer, The Canadian Press

Un juge manitobain a condamné l'ancien policier de Winnipeg Elston Bostock à une peine de sept ans de prison. Ce dernier a plaidé coupable à des accusations de trafic de drogue et de publication d'une photo d'une femme morte partiellement nue. Un juge manitobain a condamné l'ancien policier de Winnipeg Elston Bostock à une peine de sept ans de prison. Il a plaidé coupable à des accusations de trafic de drogue et de publication d'une photo d'une femme morte partiellement nue. Alors que la Couronne et les avocats de l'ancien policier avaient d'abord fait des recommandations distinctes concernant la peine, soit sept ans et un peu plus de deux ans, Elston Bostock a accepté vendredi une recommandation conjointe de peine de sept ans d'emprisonnement. Publicité C'était après que le juge Kenneth Champagne, de la Cour du Banc du Roi, eut déclaré aux avocats qu'il était enclin à alourdir la peine du défendeur en raison de l'absence de recommandations conjointes. Vendredi, le juge a indiqué qu'au début de l'audience de détermination de la peine de Bostock sa décision s'élevait à 13, 5 ans, même s'il s'attendait à ce qu'elle puisse être réduite après avoir pris en considération le principe de totalité, qui vise à éviter les peines excessives en cas de multiples chefs d'accusation. Elston Bostock a réagi en laissant échapper un juron en réaction à cette déclaration, se couvrant le visage de ses mains et secouant la tête. Lorsque les avocats sont revenus après une brève pause pour examiner ces commentaires, l'avocat de la défense Richard Wolson a déclaré à la cour qu'Elston Bostock avait accepté la recommandation commune de sept ans. Publicité Elston Bostock a plaidé coupable à une longue liste d'infractions en novembre dernier. Il a notamment admis avoir fait annuler des contraventions en échange d'alcool et de cartes-cadeaux, d'avoir volé du cannabis sur une scène de police, d'avoir transmis des informations policières confidentielles et d'avoir envoyé des messages textes obscènes concernant une photo qu'il avait prise du corps presque nu d'une femme morte d'une surdose. Ce mois-ci, l'ancien policier a admis les chefs d'accusation fédéraux d'avoir fait du trafic de cocaïne et de psilocybine, parfois vêtu de son uniforme, dans les stationnements de certains postes de police, mais aussi à partir de son propre véhicule. La peine de sept ans a été suggérée en vertu d'un accord de plaidoyer qui limitait la peine à six ans pour les accusations provinciales et à un an pour l'accusation fédérale. La défense d'Elston Bostock devait, selon l'accord, demander une peine d'au moins deux ans pour les accusations provinciales, ainsi qu'une peine consécutive de n'importe quelle durée pour l'accusation fédérale. Un jour sombre Les chefs d'accusation ont été déposés contre Elston Bostock à la suite d'une enquête qui a commencé en 2024 et qui a constaté des infractions remontant à 2016. Bien qu'Elston Bostock ait été renvoyé des forces de police, le tribunal a précédemment appris qu'il conserverait sa pension. Trois autres agents ont été inculpés aux côtés d'Elston Bostock pour des faits présumés liés à ses infractions. Un rapport psychologique préparé pour sa condamnation indique qu'il consommait de la drogue et de l'alcool pour faire face à une dépression. Il est également indiqué que, à la fin de sa carrière, il buvait et consommait de la marijuana pendant ses quarts de travail. Le juge a déclaré que les gestes du policier constituaient un jour sombre pour la confiance du public dans l'administration de la justice. Avec les informations de La Presse canadienne et Caitlyn Gowriluk

L'organisme Spectre de rue qui chapeaute le site d'injection supervisée de la rue Ontario se défend d'être inactif en expliquant qu'il y a un nombre croissant d'utilisateurs de drogues partout à Montréal. On est un peu dans l'œil du cyclone. Les gens n'ont plus de place pour rester, ils n'ont pas de soins et la drogue est de mauvaise qualité, c'est pire qu'avant la pandémie. Ça peut mettre les gens dans des états plus dangereux autant physiquement que mentalement, observe Annie Aubertin, directrice générale de Spectre de rue. Celle qui travaille au sein de l'organisme depuis six ans rapporte que le contexte des deux dernières années va au-delà de leurs effectifs. C'est indéniable qu'il y a une croissance de personnes dans la rue et une croissance de personnes qui utilisent des drogues injectables et qui sont inhalées, ajoute Mme Aubertin. En ce qui concerne la forte présence de seringues, elle souligne que des équipes font souvent des rondes mais qu'il est impossible de suivre tout le monde. Elle invite également les citoyens qui le souhaitent à suivre des formations pour apprendre à bien ramasser des seringues et à se procurer le matériel nécessaire à l'organisme. Regardez aussi ce podcast vidéo tiré de l'émission de Benoit Dutrizac, diffusée sur les plateformes QUB et simultanément sur le 99. 5 FM Montréal: Agrandissement Le centre d'injection supervisée situé sur la rue Ontario depuis 2017 offrira prochainement un service pour les consommateurs de drogues inhalées, comme le crack, un projet auquel s'oppose le Collectif Ontario à l'heure actuelle compte tenu de la situation déjà fragile. Cet agrandissement, c'est pour permettre d'accueillir des personnes qui inhalent et qui sont déjà dans notre environnement. La santé publique nous a demandé d'ouvrir une salle d'inhalation, donc on aura quatre places pour des inhalateurs, rapporte Annie Aubertin.

L'Agence des services frontaliers du Canada (ASFC) indique que ses agents ont saisi 87 kg de stupéfiants au poste frontalier de Coutts, entre l'Alberta et le Montana. La drogue devait être transportée à Calgary. L' ASFC précise dans un communiqué que la saisie a eu lieu le 15 février, à la suite d'une fouille. La marchandise illicite était contenue dans trois valises dissimulées à l'intérieur d'un camion commercial dont le chauffeur prétendait transporter des produits agricoles. Le conducteur, arrêté par des agents de l' ASFC, a depuis été placé en détention par la GRC. Publicité Janalee Bell-Boychck, directrice régionale de l' ASFC pour les Prairies, affirme que cette saisie met en évidence le rôle essentiel et constant que jouent les agents de l' ASFC pour lutter contre le crime organisé et empêcher que des drogues dangereuses atteignent les communautés de l'Alberta. L' ASFC ajoute que cet incident fait suite à 3 opérations distinctes qui ont été effectuées au même poste frontalier de Coutts à la fin de l'année dernière et qui ont permis à ses agents de mettre la main sur plus de 1000 kg de stupéfiants.

Cochrane RCMP say a Calgary man is facing multiple drug trafficking charges after an investigation that began in April 2025 and led to the seizure of more than four kilograms of suspected drugs, including fentanyl, methamphetamine and cocaine, following a search of a storage locker in Airdrie. Police say the drugs seized have an estimated street value of approximately 450, 000. Police say the Cochrane RCMP Crime Reduction Unit, with assistance from RCMP Federal Policing Northwest Region, began investigating a man suspected of trafficking drugs between Calgary and Lethbridge. RCMP say investigators later confirmed the suspect was actively involved in drug trafficking within the Stoney Nakoda First Nation community. Officers say a vehicle associated with the suspect was located on Feb. 26, 2026, at what they describe as a known problem address on the Stoney Nakoda First Nation and was towed after the registered owner claimed it had been taken without consent. Investigators say the investigation led officers to a storage locker in Airdrie that belonged to the suspect. Police say a search warrant was executed on the storage locker on March 9, 2026, where approximately 1. 4 kilograms of controlled substances were seized. The suspect was not present at the time. RCMP say the suspect was located again on March 11 at a tow yard in Cochrane, where officers from the General Investigation Section and Crime Reduction Unit, with assistance from Southern Alberta District GIS, established covert surveillance and were supported by the Emergency Response Team, RCMP Police Dog Services and Calgary Police Service's HAWCS helicopter. Officers say the suspect exited a vehicle carrying a bag and began walking away, and was arrested without incident. Investigators say a search of the bag incidental to arrest resulted in the seizure of an additional 2. 7 kilograms of suspected drugs. In total, police report seizing 581. 2 grams of suspected fentanyl, 1, 041 grams of suspected cocaine, 2, 472. 4 grams of suspected methamphetamine, 2. 2 grams of suspected carfentanil, and 6, 798 in cash. RCMP have charged Dylan Watson, 42, of Calgary with two counts each of possession for the purpose of trafficking cocaine, fentanyl and methamphetamine. Police say Watson was remanded into custody following a judicial interim release hearing and was scheduled to appear in Alberta Court of Justice in Calgary on March 12, 2026.
