TORONTO - Steam slowly spiraled up from the trays of freshly cooked meals laid on a table at the corner of the sprawling basement room. Dozens of people sat around other tables, some of them eating while others took sips of hot tea and coffee as they laughed and smiled. A small group of servers delivered plates and guided visitors to their seats. Among them was Tanja Futter, who was on the move like an attentive waitress, zigzagging around the tables, offering food and asking about everyone's day. "Why don't you take a seat there, " she told a man who wanted to eat, pointing towards a chair. Then came the plate filled with fried fish, cooked vegetables, mushrooms and fries. "Here we go. " This scene unfolded on a recent Thursday at the Sanctuary Ministries Toronto, a church in the downtown core that has provided a safe haven for the most marginalized and vulnerable for more than three decades. Here at the church on Charles Street East, just around the corner from Yonge Street people struggling with homelessness, addiction, mental heath and poverty are welcomed in to dine, take a hot shower, seek medical care, collect sleeping bags and winter clothing and, more importantly, hang out with people who remember their names. It is a community that has been "built on trust, " where everyone feels safe, said Futter, who is the pastoral director at the Sanctuary. "There is a beauty of Sanctuary where I've said to many people that this is the most transformative community I've ever been part of, " said Futter. "And it is also, you know, the most grief that I have ever experienced in my life. " She said she got to know people who died of overdoses, and has driven people to the hospital after suicide attempts. "It's the relational part that hurts more, because you actually care for people, " she said. The proximity to such struggles is not something that Sanctuary's neighbours have always tolerated. The board of CASA condos at 33 Charles Street East has filed a 2. 3-million lawsuit against Sanctuary, saying its clients have created safety risks for condo residents. In its statement of claim, the board alleges the church is allowing "illicit, disruptive, interfering and egregious conduct" including drug use and trafficking, overdoses and serious physical altercations to happen on its property, according to court documents provided by the Sanctuary. Greg Cook, an outreach team lead at the church, said he cannot comment on the lawsuit because the matter is before the court. But he said the work they do is more important than ever, given the depth of the homelessness crisis. Homelessness isn't a new problem in Ontario and in Toronto, but Cook, who has been working with the homeless population for nearly two decades, said it exploded in recent years as the cost of housing doubled while income and government assistance remained almost the same. When he started the outreach work, there was a shortage of housing, but "it felt like a possibility" for people to find it, he said. Services weren't available as widely as they are now, but not too many people needed them. That isn't the case anymore. "If your situation is you maybe have a criminal record or you have bad credit or you're living outside, the chances of getting housing is almost impossible, " he said. Citing the city's data, Cook said the number of homeless people jumped from fewer than 8, 000 in 2021 to more than 15, 000 in late 2024. The Ontario Municipalities Association says 80, 000 people experienced homelessness in 2024. Earlier this month, Ontario's Big City Mayors called on the Ontario government to declare a state of emergency to address the issue, which they said has created a "community safety and humanitarian crisis" across the province. Cook said what he does at the church makes his life more meaningful. "I'd say it's also an honour to hold people's trust, " he said, adding that between 300 and 350 community participants visit the church each week. The Canadian Press spent several Thursday evenings in November and December visiting Sanctuary and spoke with a handful of people who visit frequently to hear their histories and understand what their day-to-day lives are like. - SABRINA A white Christian family took Sabrina Wanee-Katari Sutherland and her sister into their home when she was 11 or 12 years old. Sutherland, who mainly grew up in Attawapiskat First Nation, said she had been repeatedly sexually assaulted by her mother's boyfriend. Both of them were implicated in a legal case over the alleged child abuse, and the two girls entered the provincial foster care system, eventually landing in Kingston, Ont. "Within a few months, they decided that I was more damaged than they initially thought, the foster family, " she said. The family kept her sister - with whom she had not been allowed to speak Cree - and she was sent to a group home. At 16, her access to the group home ended. The province had not yet raised the age of protection to 18, a change that would only take effect in 2018. She left for Toronto. After a one-night stand, Sutherland had an unplanned pregnancy. Four months in, she had no idea what was happening to her body. When a nurse congratulated her after seeing test results, she said she was so shocked that she "almost fell off the chair. " It brought things into perspective, and she set out to seek a better life. She went back to Kingston, gave birth to her daughter Kayla and enrolled to finish high school, where a daycare was available. Sutherland found a part-time job at a law firm. She worked there for several years and got her own apartment. Thanks to her fast typing and strong spelling skills, she became a court reporter in Kingston. She and Kayla moved back to Toronto when Kayla was in Grade 6 or 7. Sutherland found another job as a court reporter at the Federal Court, and started studying in a radio television arts university program. But then things turned upside down. Sutherland's childhood trauma began to haunt her, she said. "I would see him in cars, or if I was on the streetcar, I would see him outside, you know, on a sidewalk, " she said of her abuser. "Or I would see him hiding behind bushes and shrubs. " She quit school and left her job. She tried cocaine for the first time when out camping with a cousin. It quickly became a habit. A few years after they moved to Toronto, Sutherland sent Kayla to live with a lawyer she used to work with. She decided to embark on a cross-country journey in the hopes of finding healing and detoxing from her addiction. The last time she was housed was in 2018, Sutherland said. She had been living with a man for several years. She said he beat her, and their relationship ended badly. After the COVID-19 pandemic began, encampments began to pop up in Toronto. Sutherland said she had been living at a cottage, but she returned to the city and began splitting her time between tents and shelter beds. Today, Sutherland is 51 years old and has a fentanyl addiction. She only understands a little bit of Cree, the language she knew fluently as a child. She is HIV positive. She said she is not sure how she caught the virus, but she has faced sexual assaults, she has been beaten unconscious and she could have been exposed to a contaminated syringe. Sitting by a table in a small room at Sanctuary Toronto, Sutherland shared that she has always felt ashamed of her First Nation heritage. "I would always say I was half white and I was assimilated, " she said while combing her hair. "They are misunderstood and targeted and abused by the system. They're unwanted by society, " she said, speaking about both the homeless population and Indigenous people. "Because in the long run. . . it's more expensive to help them. It would be cheaper if they died. " Her daughter Kayla Sutherland is more hopeful. She is a well-known activist and works as an intergenerational relations program co-ordinator at the east-end Children's Peace Theatre. She visits her mother regularly at Sanctuary. "They're like my older brothers and uncles, the staff that have been taking care of my mom, " she said of the staff. She said if her mother is able to get off drugs, they are planning to enrol her in a trauma recovery program that uses Indigenous approaches and medicine. Sutherland said she has detoxed in the past, and she is ready to do it again. She wants to heal, and "self-medicating with fentanyl is not going to work. " --- TONY Tony Aguiar left his apartment this spring due to what he described as deteriorating living conditions in his supportive housing unit. He has been sleeping on cardboard in the doorway of an empty building in downtown Toronto ever since. "The owners could have asked me to leave at any time, but because I don't leave a mess, I'm not making noise, I'm not damaging the place, they allow me to stay there, " he said. "I do feel lucky. I do feel blessed. " Aguiar said he is happy he has a space where he can sleep alone, away from the noise of an encampment. Even though many people prefer to stay in a tent, Aguiar said that doesn't make him feel safe. "I don't really like tents, because you're hidden. You can't see what's going on outside around you, " he said. Aguiar added he hopes to be able to secure a hotel room that the City of Toronto is offering as a temporary shelter. He doesn't want the children at a nearby school see him every morning. "In this world, there is not much that matters to me, but the kids matter to me most, " he said, grinding his cannabis into a bowl. While living in a doorway is freezing, he stills prefers it from the shelters. "I feel a lot safer in my doorway or in a park or behind a garbage bin or somewhere where I just feel that no one has a chance to. . . (steal) my stuff, " he said. Aguiar said he doesn't use any hard drugs, but he drinks a lot of alcohol and smokes cigarettes and cannabis. He said he started drinking alcohol when he was a teenager, with his friends in downtown Toronto. At that time, his drinking habits were largely under control, he said. Then his cousin, who was very close to him, died of what he suspects was a drug overdose nearly two decades ago. The loss left him devastated, and that is when his drinking became a serious problem. The first time he became homeless, Aguiar was 17. Now, at 44, he is struggling again. "The way you think life is going to go, sometimes it doesn't go that way, " he said. "So I am kinda used to life not going the way I see it going, or the way it should go. " Aguiar said he has a 22-year-old daughter. He hasn't seen her since she was a toddler, but they speak sometimes over the phone and he often checks her Facebook page to see how she is doing. "I told her. . . that I was proud of her that she stuck with school, " he said. "Because me, I dropped out, and I just didn't make nothing of myself. " He said he hasn't seen her mother, who lives in Port Dover, Ont. , for many years. He has no intention to do so any time soon. "I don't want her to see me like this, to be honest with you, 'cause she worries too much already, " he said. Aguiar said it restores his faith in the world to see that there are people supporting the homeless community. "This world is meant for all of us to live, not some of us, " he said. - AUBREE Aubree Olson's life began plunging into a downward spiral when she picked up a serious knee injury during a basketball game in high school. At first, she took painkillers, but then turned to street drugs after the prescription ran out. Olson never finished high school. She and her father moved to Ontario from Winnipeg when she was 17. He had his own addiction issues. And after getting treatment, she said he was so fed up with his daughter's drug use that he kicked her out of the house. She was 18. "When he got out of rehab, they told him to avoid stressful situations in life, and that I was the most stressful situation in his life, " she said. "That's when our relationship ended. " A few years later, her boyfriend died of an overdose in Coburg, Ont. Olson, now 28, has been struggling with mental health, on-and-off addiction and homelessness for the past decade. Last winter, she stayed at a warming centre in Toronto, she said, but now she lives at an encampment. "I find it, like, easier to maintain my drug addiction, like to a lower level, when I am just out here by myself, " she said. She added her drug use can get "really out of control" when she is around other addicts. There are other reasons why she prefers not to live in a shelter. They feature large, overcrowded rooms where dozens of women and men are crammed in. Each has a space the size of a bed. Stealing and physical violence are common, she said. The last time Olson was kicked out of a shelter, it was because she had been engaged in a physical altercation with a man. "Staff only saw me punching him in the face. They didn't witness me getting dragged across a room by (my) hair. " As winter sets in, Olson's priorities are shifting. While she would prefer to have a space of her own, like a room at a hotel or an apartment, her No. 1 goal now is simply to find a place that has walls and a roof, so she can stay warm. "It's really cold. I don't like it, " she said. Olson said she has been able to detox several times. "Every New Year's, I would just think, OK, this is it. I'm going to quit doing drugs, " she said. "I only managed to stay off drugs for a couple of months. . . . The last time I did it was probably three years ago. " Though the experience of withdrawal is rough, she is ready to give it another try. She wants to take the nine credits she still needs to graduate from high school. Olson uses fentanyl, one of the strongest and most addictive drugs. It has one of the highest relapse rates. She is aware of that. "Most people that do fentanyl or are addicted to opioids will be addicted to them for the rest of their lives, so the statistics are not really on my side, " she said. "But I'm positive about it. " - CRYSTOFUR Crystofur Taggart became a member of Toronto's homeless community when he was just 16. "On my birthday, my foster dad gave me 300 cash, told me he didn't want to make me leave, but he had no choice, '" he remembers being told. Under a temporary care agreement, he said, the foster family with whom he had lived for three years couldn't continue to keep him in the house after he turned 16. Taggart had been in the system for several years after facing an abusive situation at home and trying to take his own life. He said he began identifying as bisexual or gay as a kid, and his parents did not approve of that. "They would always fight with me. I would always fight with them, " he said. Taggart said he got the Children's Aid Society involved through school after things got physical between him and his stepdad. "I attempted suicide when I was like 13, and Children's Aid Society came to the hospital and took me to a foster home from the hospital. " On the eve of his 16th birthday, Taggart said his foster family called youth shelters to see if they could find him a place to sleep. They had no luck. He had nowhere else to stay. His mother and stepfather had since moved away from Ontario. He ended up sleeping in the alleyway across the street from a shelter for a few nights before getting a bed. "I had never slept outside before, " he said. "I was alone. All I could really think about was that I had nobody willing to let me stay with them. " Taggart, now 28, said he has been mostly homeless and struggled with addiction since then. His partner died of a fentanyl overdose in 2020. These experiences have left him "heartbroken, " he said. Recently, Taggart said his tent at a downtown encampment under the Gardiner Expressway - and everything in it, including dog food, sleeping bag and winter clothes - was gone when he returned to it. That night, he and his dog Coco had to sleep on the concrete stairwell of a parking garage, he said. There are few options for shelter. Taggart said he has been trying to get a bed, but there is a shortage of spaces. He prefers to find a place that will allow him to be with Coco, but many places do not accept animals. "Being outside in the cold is, it's not manageable. It's not easy. It's scary. It makes my mental health worse, " he said. "It makes survival more expensive, and it's not good for my dog. " He said he now lives at another encampment after a woman bought him a tent, winter clothing and a dog coat. He said he will send Coco to stay with a friend so she can escape the unbearably freezing temperature. "I would also miss her. She's my best friend. But her well-being is what I care about most, " he said, as the white-and-black dog lay snoring under a table by his feet. Taggart's biological father lives in poverty in Ontario, and he can't expect any support from him, he said. His mother, who now lives in the United States, will not take him in. He said she told him she fears he would fall into "bad habits" and need medical help - "and it's not free here. " Taggart gets 700 monthly from the government. He said it is impossible to secure permanent housing with that amount. Homeless people and those on social assistance are discriminated against when they apply for housing, he said. When he sends messages to rental property managers and owners, he usually does not get a reply. - If you or someone you know is thinking about suicide, support is available 247 by calling or texting 988, Canada's national suicide prevention helpline. A months-long RCMP investigation that began with suspected drug runs between Calgary and Canmore has resulted in four arrests and nearly half a million dollars in drugs and weapons seized. Cochrane RCMP began investigating a man suspected of trafficking drugs between Calgary and Canmore in March 2026. Officers later confirmed he was transporting wholesalelevel drugs from Calgary into the Bow Valley. On March 13, police stopped a vehicle linked to the suspect and seized 1, 097 grams of fentanyl. The investigation continued on May 14, when officers executed a search warrant at a Canmore home, finding 1. 6 kilograms of fentanyl and cocaine along with 2, 000 counterfeit Xanax tablets. Two Canmore residents, Mackenzie Harbar, 30, and Katie Ervin, 31, were charged. Harbar also faces breach of conditions charges. RCMP seizure of fentanyl after trafficking investigation. (Cochrane RCMP) Evidence from the Canmore search led officers to open a second investigation in Calgary. Police executed two search warrants in the city on May 27, seizing 0. 5 kilograms of fentanyl and cocaine, more than 1, 100 syntheticopioid tablets, and a prohibited firearm. Two Calgary residents, Aaron Cahoon, 30, and Jordan Nyiro, 31, were charged with drug trafficking offences. Nyiro also faces firearms charges. In total, police seized 1, 186 grams of fentanyl, 915 grams of cocaine, 2, 895 counterfeit opioid pills, 7 grams of methamphetamine, and a semiautomatic rifle and prohibited magazines. Police estimate the total street value at about 490, 000.

The B. C. Coroners Service has released data on drug deaths in April, including in Langley. (File photo) LANGLEY ADVANCE TIMES - Langley has seen four more people die from the toxic street drug supply, according to the B. C. Coroners Service. The latest report on the ongoing public health crisis said that as of the end of April, Langley has seen 14 drug deaths in total. The last report from the B. C. Coroners Service said that as of the end of March, 10 drug deaths had been recorded locally. Unfortunately, this means Langley is not seeing a decline in drug deaths. At this rate, the community is on track to see about 42 deaths this year. That is in the same range that Langley has seen in recent years. Between 2020 and 2025, Langley saw anywhere between 37 and 56 deaths annually. The deaths are caused by high-potency drugs, particularly opioids like fentanyl, which arrived in the street drug supply a decade ago, sharply increasing the number of deaths among users. In 2015, Langley saw 10 deaths by overdoses or toxic drugs. The following year, that number jumped to 31. Across the province, 119 people died in April, according to the Coroners Service's preliminary numbers. As usual, a large majority - 68 per cent - were between the ages of 30 and 59, and 76 per cent were men. The mix of drugs continues to change. So far in 2026, fluorofentanyl, a chemical analogue of fentanyl, was the ingredient most commonly found in tested street drugs, with 67 per cent of samples positive for the substance. Cocaine was second (57 per cent) followed by fentanyl (56 per cent). Methamphetamine and number of illicit prescription drugs made up the remaining common ingredients. - Matthew Claxton is a reporter with the Langley Advance Times ------------ Sign up for our newsletter Don't miss out on reading the latest top stories from the Langley Advance Times. One person is suspected to have died, and there have been dozens of overdoses from a new supply of tainted fentanyl found in the Region of Waterloo. That's according to the Region's Public Health department's latest drug alert, issued Thursday. It said 36 cases came in the five days from Feb. 21 to 25. The alert said everyone needs to "be cautious using yellow, dark orange, or dark blue drugs. " It went on to say some people using these drugs reported memory loss, confusion and being very sleepy. According to Sanguen's drug checking program, fentanyl samples of concern have medetomidine, benzodiazepines, xylazine, and nitazenes "unexpectedly mixed in. These drugs increase risk of overdose. " The alert said naloxone should still be given in a suspected overdose, but it can not stop the effects of non-opioid drugs like most of those additives. All of those additives can cause deep sedation, known as being "on the nod. " They can also cause hallucinations, blackouts, and very low or no pulse. All users are reminded they can call 911 in the event of finding someone having an overdose.

Copper wire thefts continue to be an issue right across Canada, but it's hitting especially close to home in Waterloo Region. Businesses in Cambridge, most notably near Hwy. 401, say the crime is becoming all too common. Cambridge Ward 1 Councillor Helen Shwery took to social media saying copper wire thefts are a "huge" problem in the city and is trying to raise awareness. The rise in thefts prompted Connie Cody, the Conservative MP for Cambridge to push for a crackdown on scrap yards that buy stolen copper wire. Last month, she introduced a private member's bill in the House of Commons that would make it a crime for scrap metal dealers to trade, traffic or have for sale any scrap metal that was known to be stolen, punishable by a fine of up to 10, 000 and a jail sentence of up to two years. Waterloo Regional Police Chief Mark Crowell told The Mike Farwell Show on 570 NewsRadio they are very much aware of the issue. "Even for a small piece of scrap metal coming out of air conditioner units and so on, can be tens of thousands of dollars of damage for a couple hundred of dollars of metal, " said Crowell. "It's often a small network of people that are either local, or coming to take advantage of opportunities within the region so the ongoing reporting is crucial. We have multiple projects, we are focusing on prolific offenders, people known to be involved and we have made some significant arrests and investigative inroads. " In January, Waterloo regional police charged two men in Kitchener with a long list of offences in connection with copper theft. "Sometimes it's acts of desperation where people are simply trying to fuel you know whether it can be a drug addiction or some of those legitimate survival concerns, but most often this is a coordinated organized crime. " Crowell adds the copper wire thefts often fuel other organized crime practices.

Part of reporter Jenny Lamothe's role with Sudbury. com is reporting on homelessness and issues within the most vulnerable sectors of our community. In this year-end column, she shares some thoughts on the past year of the crisis A tent on the east side of the Energy Court encampment is shown on a sunny but cold Dec. 17. 1 1 A tent on the east side of the Energy Court encampment is shown on a sunny but cold Dec. 17. Advertisement I'm supposed to write a year-end review of the homelessness crisis in Sudbury. I don't think I know how; not anymore, anyway. I feel like I've written it too many times. Over and over, the same story, sometimes even at the expense of stories I'd love to write. The frontline workers of Sudbury - and frontline is an apt description for the battle they face each day - don't have it in them anymore, but they keep going, so maybe I can write a few more words. Cycle and cycle: Homelessness, drugs, addiction, crime, jail, homelessness, drugs, addiction, crime, jail, repeat. Groundhog Day in Greater Sudbury. Sometimes, I think it's that government policy won't pick a side. Either it's evidence-based, or it's morality-based, but either way, only in half measure. Sometimes, I think death is the feature, not the bug. And if you know me, you know that I am an annoyingly positive person. I don't lose hope easily and while this is certainly not my final bow, I have to admit this cycle hurts. It's the one I hit almost every year when I try to write an article that encompasses some of the biggest stories of the past 365 days and I inevitably hit the themes of homelessness and opioids. Encampments dismantled, then again, and again; consultants hired, a Summit and plans made, then, three years later, plans abandoned. Safe sites opened, safe sites closed, more tents, new encampments. At one point, I thought if I just wrote it the right way, people would understand. Silly, I know. I can be a little romantic. I spent three months interviewing and writing a feature article in 2023, hoping to point to the cause and effect of the crises. Everything I wrote is still applicable, we could have written it yesterday. Because now I hear involuntary care, when I have yet to hear there is enough room for voluntary care. I hear people call for criminalizing a health care issue, trying to treat substance use in jail, with the ill-informed idea that there are no drugs inside. A report from the John Howard Society shows that drug toxicity was the most frequently identified cause of death for those who died in custody between 2014 and 2021, approximately 40 per cent of all deaths in custody recorded for that period. Policing open drug use and sending people right back into hiding, where they began dying in droves: enough people died that all three levels of government declared a crisis. But, did we ever move far enough in one direction to decide to reverse abruptly and move in the other? Just after the closure of Sudbury's supervised consumption site in March, 2024, an outreach worker told me "When you close a supervised consumption site, the city becomes an unsupervised consumption site. " She was correct. And now, it seems we are back to the beginning of the cycle. The people who use drugs hide, and they die. Most of the overdose deaths that now occur in Sudbury are in private residences. But it's the open use that makes people nervous, watching someone shoot up or slump over in a haze, but really, because there is nowhere else for them to use. They are homeless, likely now living in Energy court. Most of them are local. In 2024, 72 per cent of a survey of homeless people in Sudbury stated they had been in Sudbury for more than five years. There are also multiple generations. Let me tell you about a family I know. I met the patriarch of the family at the Warming Centre in 2021. Three months ago, I met this man's two sons, who are living in the Energy Court encampment. His youngest son, 29, and I talked for a while about his set-up, which was designed thoughtfully and earnestly - honestly, the survival skills on display in community are incredible - and then he mentioned his own kids. He had four, between the ages of five and 12, and said he hoped to get them out of foster care one day. An outreach worker once told me that aging out of foster care - becoming a legal adult at age 18 and losing access to many of the supports available - is referred to as "graduating into homelessness. " Statistically, his children are 30 per cent more likely to enter homelessness themselves. In fact, in a survey completed by 229 people who were homeless in Sudbury sometime between Oct. 8-15, 2024, showed 35 per cent of respondents had been in foster care or a youth group home, with 24 per cent becoming homeless within 30 days of leaving foster caregroup home. And though the research into the connection is limited, a 2014 study out of Vancouver showed even then that among a sample of 937 people aged 14-26 who use illicit drugs, 455 (49 per cent) reported being in government care at some point in their childhood. These statistics are much worse for children of Indigenous parents, who are disproportionately affected by both the opioids and homelessness crises. All this, in addition to the knowledge that their dad lives in a tent in the middle of winter in the centre of a town that does not hide secrets well. And beyond the abhorrent idea that the death of these people is a solution to anything, you might see we're already too far in. It's too big for us to fail. We can't just let this "take care of itself, " we can't police it into submission, and certainly, we can't coddle it either. But I'm scared. I'm scared that if I have the good fortune to be a journalist in another five years, I'll be writing this story again, but it will be worse. It will be catastrophic. The thing is, there is another cycle of things I write. The answers given so often by the subjects of my articles about homelessness: we need housing, health care and income supplements. It's almost like maintaining and then criminalizing poverty. We maintain it through low minimum wages and stagnant disability support. If the experiences of the people I've spoken with over the last five years tell me anything, almost everything that happens after you can't pay your bills is usually a crime, as is the substance many choose to deal with living rough. And if it was trauma that sent someone into the wanting hands of the streets five years ago, it's been burning through them for that much longer, corroding them from the inside. That, and the loss of dozens of friends from overdose. I've only been on the cusp of this crisis and I have loved and lost five people to toxic poisoning. I met them out on the street in my work as a reporter, built trust as best I could so I could lift their voices and as you would expect, they helped me to build mine. Then in a second, gone. I've said all this and I still don't know what to say. Sudbury. com's editor, Mark Gentili says "you have to know the story in one sentence or you don't know the story. " I know the story, and man, I just want to know how it ends. Beard said Mounties were involved in "quite a cross-section of events" over the three-month span. Of the detachment's 5, 740 files, 1, 229 - or 22 per cent - originated within Duncan city limits. "We were involved in some exciting things, some fun things, and some traumatic things, " said the commanding officer. Beard said officers dealt with a wide range of incidents during the quarter, similar to those in other areas of the province. He noted increases in property crime were largely driven by shoplifting, thefts, thefts from vehicles and mischief, with most incidents involving repeat offenders rather than organized retail crime groups. Beard said violent crimes increased 58 per cent and were often linked to public disorder, substance use, mental-health issues and housing instability. One unusual robbery attempt, Beard highlighted, was when a suspect used a stick to demand money from shopkeepers. The suspect was arrested. Another specific case was a drug-related assault that involved a person the victim being struck over the back of the head and their belongings taken. Sexual assault files increased to nine from one in the same quarter of 2025. Six involved family or intimate-partner relationships and none were stranger assaults. Beard noted a 325 per cent increase in frauds compared to the same period in 2025, with 17 files reported between January and March, up from four the previous year. Most involved online scams, including phishing and spoofing schemes designed to mimic legitimate bank or Canada Revenue Agency websites. In one case, an elderly victim left a bank card in an ATM and a suspect used it at several businesses around Duncan. Police identified the suspect through video surveillance and have recommended charges. Mischief calls rose 122 per cent, increasing by 62 files. Most reports involved property-related disturbances, unwanted gatherings, loitering and disruptions to the use of public spaces. Many incidents were concentrated near the Silver Bridge and river area, extending toward Trunk Road, with peaks in the early morning and late evening. Calls for service increased 20 per cent during the first three months of 2026, representing roughly 1, 000 additional calls. Beard's report also referenced a January meeting of community leaders focused on addressing racism in the region. Beard's update also included mention of a January meeting of community leadership groups to discuss the rise of racism in the region. "Leadership has a responsibility to confront racism when they see it and model attitudes, communicate values and demonstrate actions that reflect an unwillingness to accept that behavior, " he said. The report also noted officers are active along the Trans-Canada Highway Corridor and on Lewis Street. The report highlighted two traffic stops in February and March that resulted in the seizure of drugs, illegal cigarettes, stolen property, cash and weapons. One vehicle linked to alleged drug trafficking was forfeited to the B. C. Civil Forfeiture Office, and charges are pending.

In Portage la Prairie and across rural Manitoba the pressure on addictions supports and homelessness services continues to grow. Portage la Prairie MLA, Deputy Opposition leader, and Critic of Addictions and Homelessness Jeff Bereza steps forward to discuss how the proposed provincial legislation and local readiness are shaping up, what questions remain unanswered, and how his office is pushing for greater clarity and accountability. Bill 48's scope and intent Bereza notes that the new legislation, Bill 48: Detention and Care of Intoxicated Persons Act, is aimed at extending the hold on intoxicated individuals from 24 hours to 72 hours, and is proposed to include people with drug addictions in addition to those who have over-consumed alcohol. He notes this is, generally speaking, a good plan; however, there is a "but. . . " He adds that while alcohol intoxication typically resolves within a day, the "psychosis that they're in can last for days and days" in cases involving methamphetamine or fentanyl. He continues that the essential question is who will care for these individuals after 72 hours and whether supports "and the facilities are there. " Rural readiness and transparency concerns Bereza says there is concern that the bill will apply not just in Winnipeg but in rural areas as well, and asks what happens if "every bed is full. " He notes that local agencies and municipalities face a lack of transparency around how many staff will be required, what qualifications they must have, and how many beds will be available. He adds that while the province says a facility will open in three weeks, "we don't even know what a protective-care facility is right now. " Local impacts in Portage la Prairie Bereza continues that in his riding the involvement of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, community safety officers, and stretched-thin resources raise major logistical questions. He says that even if a person is picked up under the act, "the first 24 hours they can stay in the cell, but the other 48 hours they need to be moved to a protective-care unit and be assessed by someone. " He adds that Portage may have to send someone "to Winnipeg" because no local unit is yet confirmed, and the RCMP officers are already stretched. Legislative process and stakeholder engagement Bereza notes that during committee hearings dozens of people sought to speak but were repeatedly denied leave by the governing party, even though the bill "is probably one of the most critical pieces of legislation that we'll see over the next couple of years. " He adds that they plan to introduce a number of amendments to strengthen the transparency and clarity around Bill 48. He continues that without a clear plan "this could be chaotic, " and that so far the government has given little indication of what will change. The broader challenge of addiction and homelessness Bereza says the crisis goes beyond the law and into education, prevention and treatment - noting that the equivalent of a fatal fentanyl dose could be "smaller than two grains of salt. " He adds that making a real dent in the issue means helping people get off drugs, supporting affordable housing, and addressing underlying poverty and theft fuelled by addiction. He continues that "it is absolutely not about money" but about getting the implementation right, especially if workers, supports, and facilities are lacking. Related stories: Moving forward and next steps Bereza says crews in his team will continue monitoring Bill 48's implementation, pushing for clarity about what protective-care units look like, how many staff are available, and what rural Manitoba's role will be. He adds that if the government rushes to pass the legislation without ensuring the supports are in place, "we're just creating an in-and-out system" where people walk out the door and end up right back in. Penticton News South Okanagan MP calls out rise in overdose response while supporting court-ordered rehab bill MP: City 'filled with chaos' Photo: Helena Konanz (FacebookFile photo) Helena Konanz in Ottawa. Local MP Helena Konanz spoke in support of a bill that would allow judges to enforce court-ordered rehabilitation on an offender, saying her hometown of Penticton is "filled with chaos" due to rising overdose and public safety calls. The Similkameen-South Okanagan-West Kootenay area MP spoke on Monday during a House of Commons debate regarding the second reading of Bill C-240. Bill C-240 would amend the Criminal Code and the Controlled Drugs and Substances Act, and make related amendments to the Corrections and Conditional Release Act. The bill, introduced by Kitchener Centre MP Kelly DeRidder, seeks to allow courts to mandate rehabilitative measures for offenders during incarceration. Konanz said this bill is important to her, as "cities have changed, including all communities in the Similkameen-South Okanagan-West Kootenay riding. " She referred to the police and bylaws' standard quarterly update recently presented to Penticton council, which saw the largest jump in service for the Penticton Fire Department being overdose responses. Incidents surged by an increase of 484 per cent compared to the first quarter of 2025. "Imagine what being a first responder in Penticton is like right now, when all they are doing is constantly going out to calls and trying to bring people back to life, " she said. "Our first responders are constantly going out and injecting people with some type of drug to try to bring them back to life. Sometimes they are successful, and sometimes they are not. " She said Interior Health and the fire department have flagged a new type of drug called Metatomidine, a sedative that is used in veterinary medicine, that is making the response "much more difficult and more prolonged. " Konanz also pointed out the notable lack of inpatient detox in Penticton, which means those who want it need to travel to neighbouring communities. City council has requested the province for support and investment to "strengthen the detox, treatment and recovery continuum in Penticton, with a focus on establishing lower-barrier transitional housing, establishing local inpatient withdrawal management and expanding treatment and recovery housing. " Konanz claimed when she was a city councillor a couple of years ago, she was told Okanagan Correctional Centre was only a quarter full. Back in February, the Ministry of Public Safety confirmed to Castanet that OCC has 401 cells with a daily average of 200 residents in 2025. Konanz said she wants to see correctional centres "provide rehabilitation measures, education, skills training and treatment. " The motion for second reading was adopted unanimously by the House and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Human Rights.

Acetaminophen remains recommended treatment in Canada for fever and pain during pregnancy Health Canada says there is "no conclusive evidence" that using acetaminophen as directed during pregnancy causes autism or other neurodevelopmental disorders. Canada's health agency released the advisory after U. S. President Donald Trump urged pregnant Americans not to use acetaminophen, known widely as Tylenol, claiming it can cause autism in unborn children. During a press conference on Monday, Trump said effective immediately, the U. S. Food and Drug Administration will notify American physicians that the use of acetaminophen during pregnancy can be associated with a "very increased risk of autism. " Across the border, Health Canada continues to recommend acetaminophen to treat pain or fever in pregnancy when used as directed. "(Acetaminophen) should be used at the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration needed. Untreated fever and pain in pregnant women can pose risks to the unborn child, " said Health Canada in an online public advisory. "Acetaminophen is commonly used to relieve pain and reduce fever. It has been used safely by millions of Canadians for decades, including during pregnancy and while breastfeeding. " Dr. Peter Bouch, with Red Deer Primary Care Network, said acetaminophen has been studied for years, and two huge studies have shown no connection between the painkiller and autism - a study in Sweden of more than two million children, and a Japanese study of 200, 000 children. Trump referenced a review article that was dismissed by a lot of medical professionals around the world, the doctor said. "I think a lot of pregnant ladies were probably stressed when they heard that, " said Bouch, referring to Trump's warning about Tylenol that has prompted a lot of discussion. The Red Deer doctor said Tylenol remains the safest anti-inflammatory to use during pregnancy, compared to Advil, Aleve and Naproxen, which can be quite dangerous for the baby. But as with any medication taken during pregnancy, Tylenol use should be limited to as little as possible. Women should also speak to their doctors if they have any questions, Bouch added. Health Canada said its advice is based on robust, rigorous assessments of the available scientific evidence. Any new evidence that could affect our recommendations will be carefully evaluated. "Health Canada monitors the safety of all medicines authorized for use in Canada, including acetaminophen. All Canadian non-prescription acetaminophen products already carry clear warnings about safe use during pregnancy and breastfeeding, as well as the risk of serious liver injury if too much is taken. " The national agency said if new scientific evidence demonstrates a risk, it would take action to update labels, inform health care professionals, and provide advice to Canadians. More on the safe use of acetaminophen and potential health risks to make informed decisions is available from Health Canada.

Salmon Arm News City of Salmon Arm's three-year youth resilience strategy coming to a close Youth program wrapping up Photo: Luc Rempel After more than three years of work Salmon Arm's youth resilience strategy is wrapping up with good news for ongoing youth support in the city. The City of Salmon Arm says it is wrapping up a three-year youth resilience strategy that supported more than 600 vulnerable youth thanks to more than 800, 000 in federal government grants. At the June 8 council meeting, Sarah Zuidof, building safer communities coordinator, gave a presentation about the city's youth resilience strategy, which ran from 2023 to 2026. Public Safety Canada awarded the city 829, 000 in grant funding to combat gangs and gun violence through the Building Safer Communities Fund about four years ago. "I remember I think it was Councillor Kevin Flynn who said, 'Why on earth would we be chosen for this kind of funding, ' and I think that was the question that many of us had, " Zuidof said. "But today, that answer is much clearer. . . . In recent years, we've witnessed the largest drug bust in all of Canada's history, only like 35 to 40 minutes from city hall. " Zuidof also highlighted news reports of gang-related activity in nearby cities like Kamloops, Vernon and Kelowna. "All of these realities, and much more, have reinforced a very important truth that no community is immune, and that prevention and community safety is really essential, " Zuidof said. "Through this last three and a half years, we've come to better understand the evolving and highly complex nature of organized crime. " She said today's gang activity extends beyond the stereotypes and intersects with elements like the dark web, human trafficking, contraband tobacco, online gaming platforms and social media. Zuidof said Indigenous and racialized youth, as well as youth not attending school or employed, are the most vulnerable to gangs and criminal influence. She said over the last three years, 647 youth were directly supported through programs funded by the grant, including wraparound support, "which is really critical for community safety. " "We've had 39 organizations participate in this initiative, and each month 20 organizations come together to form the Shuswap Youth Services Collaborative, and it's involved in many, many different professional development and collective learning activities, " Zuidhof said. Fund 'a catalyst' for change Zuidhof said the Building Safer Communities Fund has resulted in five ongoing projects, including the Shuswap Youth Services collaborative, The Hive, Secwepemc cultural camps run by Rise Up Indigenous Wellness, positive programming run by the Adams Lake Indian Band, and the Launch Youth Employment Centre. Since the city received the original 829, 000 in grant funding, Zuidhof said they have raised an additional 2. 9 million which is already being used to fund youth and community activities. "For every 1 that was invested in our community, an additional 3. 53 was secured to strengthen opportunities and supports for our local youth, " she said. "Now the Building Safer Communities Initiative has become a catalyst for lasting local change, and that's what we want to celebrate today. " She said youth resiliency is what's known as a "wicked problem" in the planning and policy world, a term used to. describe a problem with so many interconnected and complex pieces it is impossible to solve it with a single idea or organization. "The only meaningful response is through collective action, and so together we each hold a piece of the puzzle, " she said. Zuidof thanked mayor, council and city staff for their willingness to accept the grant funding and move ahead with the youth initiative. "Your leadership and your vision and your willingness to accept Public Safety Canada's money and invest in prevention has transformed this little initiative from a grant funded project into a community movement. " Coun. David Gonella said he was surprised to consider gang activity happening in Salmon Arm. "It's pretty eye opening when you think that we have gang activity in the city, " he said. "You don't really see people with colours, or like gang jackets or whatever, so to know that it's still organized here is pretty eye opening. " Mayor Alan Harrison said the work accomplished by Building Safer Communities in Salmon Arm is thanks to Zuidhof's leadership. "You've made a difference, and I know that you're going to continue to work in the field, " he said. Zuidhof said all the projects created through the BSCF are sustainable and will continue operating in Salmon Arm, noting Rise Up Indigenous Wellness is the recipient of a new 1. 5 million grant for youth and crime prevention to continue developing youth resilience in the region.

Testimony in the inquest into the Sudbury Jail death of Justin Alexander Trudeau of Wiikwemikoong came to a close Oct. 23, with a post-mortem examination revealing a drug-resistant bacterial infection, one so severe it caused septic shock and later, multi-organ failure A member of Wiikwemikoong Unceded Territory, Justin Alexander Trudeau died at the Sudbury District Jail on Feb. 13, 2021. On the last day of the inquest into his death, the jury heard he died of an infection so severe his fluid-filled lungs were three to four times their normal weight. It was an infection so "dramatic" said the pathologist who testified, it caused septic shock and multi-organ failure. Ongoing since Oct. 20, the five-person inquest jury charged with making recommendations have heard testimony from an on-call physician, health care staff at the jail, and the corrections officers who were on shift the night Trudeau died. The final day of testimony included the Sudbury-based forensic pathologist who performed Trudeau's autopsy, Dr. Martin Queen, as well as an expert in infectious disease and internal medicine, Dr. Dominc Mertz. Queen was the lead forensic pathologist in Sudbury (now partially retired) and testified Oct. 23 that he found no injuries relevant to Trudeau's cause of death, including the wounds on his hands for which he was initially prescribed antibiotics. He also found no indications of broken or injured ribs. In her testimony on Oct. 21, Chantal Shambrook, health care manager at the jail in 2021, testified she received a medical request form from Trudeau, in which he indicated he had rib pain. "There was zero evidence of any rib fractures. . . . I'm wondering if the chest discomfort he was experiencing was actually from his bad pneumonia, " said Queen. Queen said lungs are normally "light and fluffy, because they're mostly full of air, " but when an infection like this occurs, the lungs become heavy, firm and dense. "The lungs have a consistency that's similar to liver, " he said. Trudeau had acute suppurative pneumonia, said Queen: "acute" meaning it was fairly new, and "suppurative" meaning his lungs were forming or discharging pus, the thick fluid that builds up due to infection and inflammation. The man's lungs weighed a kilogram at the time of his death, three or four times its normal weight. "That's the reason the lungs were so heavy and dense and firm, " he said. "Because a significant amount of both lungs were filled basically with pus and fluid. " As part of the post-mortem, Queen said there was "wide testing for viruses, including COVID, " which were all negative. He told the jury that his examination also included culturing, a procedure used to grow and identify microorganisms like bacteria or fungi from a bodily sample. In Trudeau's case, the post-mortem specifically examined sections of lung, blood and cells from the nasopharynx, the far back of the nasal cavity where it connects to the throat. There was no fungal growth present, said Queen, but in both the lung and the blood sample, "abnormal lung tissue caused heavy growth of a methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. " That bacteria is commonly called "MRSA". Queen said Staphylococcus aureus is a "very common bacteria, " one that "about one in three people that are just out in the community" have on their skin or in their nasal cavity. "The vast, vast majority of times, it doesn't cause any problems, you don't even know it's there, " he said. "But in contrast to the normal, regular Staphylococcus aureus, there's a genetically different type, " he said, and that's MRSA. He called it a "smart bacteria" that "figured out how to get resistant to some of these newer antibiotics, including methicillin. " Queen said because of its antibiotic resistance, a MRSA infection is "much harder to treat, and therefore it can be much more dangerous and much more deadly. " He also said there are certain circumstances where the problematic bacteria is more likely to be found: "intravenous drug addicts, people with suppressed immune systems and people in crowded situations like jails, where it also may be relatively unhygienic. " But Trudeau's MRSA infection was so advanced the bacteria "migrated into his bloodstream", said the pathologist, causing septic shock. This shock caused a drop in blood pressure which resulted in a lack of blood flow and oxygen to the vital organs. Queen said the result of this domino-effect was "multi-organ failure. " Queen testified he believed Trudeau's infection had been going on "maybe five to seven days, plus or minus, " adding that "the pneumonia was probably already brewing, although it was still in a relatively early phase at that point. " Queen was then asked how long Trudeau had been dead when he was found, with testimony so far noting no CPR could be performed as he could not be moved, noting that he was found in severe rigor, Queen said that using rigor mortis, the stiffening of the muscles after death was a "rather poor and unscientific way to establish the time of death, " due to the number of variables in individuals and circumstances. "So the best I would say, is if he was really stiff when he was first found deceased, he probably had been dead for at least a few hours. " The jury then heard from Dr. Dominic Mertz, who has extensive academic and clinical experience with internal medicine and infectious disease, and based on his credentials was certified as an expert. He's also the associate editor of the Journal of Association of Medical Microbiology and infectious disease Canada. In his testimony, he pointed to the pandemic and its diagnostic challenges, testifying that pre and post-COVID a fever would see more diagnostic testing, but that care was limited by distancing requirements and staffing-shortages at the jail. "If I saw a patient with fever and I have no clue what's going on based on symptoms - or any other clear focus of infection - then I would check their chest for sure, " said Mertz. "And if someone reports fevers or chills and some level of coughing or shortness of breath or chest discomfort, " he said he would also perform further testing. In the hospital or clinic setting, with a living patient, pneumonia is commonly diagnosed by testing "sputum" said Mertz, referring to the thick fluid (mucus) coughed up from the lungs and airways, also known as phlegm. Trudeau's sample would have been cultured and likely shown MRSA growth, said Mertz. The test can take up to two days for results. But Mertz added that if a health-care provider is "sufficiently concerned that the patient has a bacterial infection and the patient's really sick, then often, I would say, more often than not: you cover for MRSA as well. " Mertz did not examine Trudeau but said after reviewing the documentation that he was probably admitted Feb. 8, 2021 with the infection, but "likely, " only had a fever. Trudeau had his vitals signs documented on Feb. 9, all of which were within range, but his fever continued until Feb. 11, but for one normal reading. Then, by Feb. 12, 2021, Trudeau's reading came up too low: hypothermia. "Hypothermia, as I mentioned, can be one of the signs of sepsis, typically a more severe sepsis, when your body isn't able anymore to produce a normal body temperature, " said Mertz. " And it looks like this is what occurred the day before his death. So probably some increased rate of progression between Feb. 11 and 12. " Mertz said constant monitoring isn't necessary for someone who is "perfectly fine, " but anyone who has a fever or an ongoing infection managed by the jail should have vital signs taken regularly; he testified that when Trudeau's temperature reading came in low, a check of his heart rate could have revealed that it was beating "very fast, " and that his blood pressure was likely "soft. " Queen also testified that the infected lungs could have been identified by using a stethoscope to listen to them. "It's possible that they may have heard some abnormal noises when they listened to his chest, " and that blood work could have indicated an issue. Mertz testified that this information could have triggered further medical investigation, "but it looked like that wasn't done, and they were satisfied with one single temperature, which wasn't normal, but they didn't recheck it. " He noted that a low temperature reading could be a sign of improper measurement, the solution for which is to simply repeat it. "If it's again too low, then I would worry, " he said. After his testimony in chief, Emily Bradley, counsel for the Ministry of the Solicitor General asked Mertz whether Dr. Moudgil, who did not examine Trudeau but prescribed him antibiotics (through a registered nurse on staff at the jail), had been advised of the change in Trudeau's temperature. Mertz said Moudgil was not made aware of any changes to Trudeau's medical condition. In response to a jury question, Mertz detailed the symptoms that would, in his mind, trigger the consideration that Trudeau didn't have the coronavirus, but instead, something more deadly. He said it was the hypothermia and sepsis "the increased heart rate and lowering blood pressure" that "he would not have expected from a COVID infection. " Though the inquest was expected to continue Friday, the testimony has now finished and was closed with a ceremony from elder Dorothy Fox of Wiikwemkoong Unceded First Nation. The inquest will not reconvene officially until Monday at 9: 30 a. m. at which time elder Fox will again open with Anishnaabe ceremony. Testimony from the two previous days can be read here and here. Saskatchewan's child and youth advocate is raising concerns about increasingly complex challenges facing young people, as well as emerging dangers linked to the province's illicit drug crisis. Dr. Lisa Broda tabled the 2025 annual report from the Saskatchewan Advocate for Children and Youth on April 29, marking her first report since beginning a second term in the role. Growing complexity in child welfare cases The report points to a continued rise in the complexity and urgency of issues affecting children and youth across multiple systems, including health, education and child welfare. Broda said many cases now involve layered challenges that are becoming harder to resolve for both her office and service providers. A key issue identified in 2025 was inadequate case management and planning, with some cases failing to properly address risks or meet the needs of children. The report also cites ongoing service gaps and staffing shortages as contributing factors. These pressures have led to delays in assessments, long waitlists and, in some instances, an inability to meet policy or legislative requirements. Investigation into child welfare practices In response, the advocate's office has launched a systemic investigation into case practices within the Ministry of Social Services and its partner agencies. The review will examine oversight and support for frontline workers, with a focus on ensuring staff have the tools and resources needed to meet their responsibilities to children. This work is expected to continue through 2026. Related Stories: Drug crisis posing risks to young children The report also highlights early findings from a separate investigation into the impact of toxic illicit drugs on young children. Substances such as fentanyl, methamphetamine and cocaine were identified as the most common risks affecting children under five. Broda warned that even small amounts of these substances can be deadly. Young children are especially vulnerable due to behaviours such as crawling and hand-to-mouth contact, which increase the risk of exposure to contaminated surfaces. The report urges the public to remain vigilant and report situations where children may be at risk. Progress and advocacy efforts Alongside identifying challenges, the report outlines progress on recommendations aimed at improving safeguards for medically vulnerable children, strengthening oversight in private placements and enhancing services in independent schools. Broda emphasized the importance of government action in implementing these recommendations to improve outcomes for young people. The report also notes the office's broader advocacy work at the national and international level. As president of the Canadian Council of Child and Youth Advocates, Broda contributed to federal discussions on a national strategy for children and youth and supports for those aging out of care. Meanwhile, the office's Youth Advisory Council provided input to the United Nations on access to education, amplifying the voices of Saskatchewan youth on a global stage. Independent oversight role The Advocate for Children and Youth operates independently from government, reporting directly to Saskatchewan's legislative assembly. The office works to ensure the rights, well-being and voices of children and youth are respected and supported across the province.

Roots on First manager Dave Mitchell was joined with Canadian Mental Health Association (CMHA) Cariboo Chilcotin Branch interim director of housing and harm reduction Michelle Stevens and executive director Tereena Donahue at a Committee of Whole Council meeting on Tuesday, June 16. (Rebecca DyokWilliams Lake Tribune) An expansion of programs and services like Jubilee House would be beneficial in Williams Lake, said the executive director of the Canadian Mental Health Association (CMHA) Cariboo Chilcotin Branch. Just 10 beds are available at the 24-hour supported program providing care for adults living with severe and persistent mental illness andor substance use challenges, noted Tereena Donahue, confirming a long wait list on Tuesday, June 16 at a Committee of Whole Council meeting. "It's a great program, the unfortunate piece is that there's not much turnover, " Donahue said. "If there's one area that I think as a community we could benefit from more housing resources, it would be on that spectrum. " At the meeting on Tuesday, June 16, Donahue shared further updates on housing initiatives and other supports to mayor and council, alongside CMHA Cariboo Chilcotin Branch interim director of housing and harm reduction Michelle Stevens and Roots on First manager Dave Mitchell. Donahue said CMHA has been offering services in Williams Lake since 1971. "It's no secret that the shelter has become one of our most visible programs, but it's only one piece of the housing continuum that we provide, and housing is only one piece of the broader spectrum of the services that we're providing, " Donahue added. "Roots on First is quite visible because homelessness is visible, but we see Roots on First as a doorway, as an interconnection into our community and as a connection to CMHA's programs, community services, healthcare, income supports, housing options and to relationships that someone might have to go towards stability. " The housing continuum doesn't start with Roots on First, according to Donahue, but with their homeless outreach program. The program involves a full-time staff member actively building relationships with people in the community who are experiencing homelessness or are on the streets or in encampments. Supported independent housing is also provided by the CMHA Cariboo Chilcotin Branch, which supports about 75 individuals with rental subsidies to help access and maintain market rentals. For some people, financial support is all they need, Donahue said, while others need more. That's where the CMHA Cariboo Chilcotin Branch's other programs and supports come into play. Jubilee Place, which is currently in the process of relocating its residents in order to be redeveloped by BC Housing into supportive housing, provides transitional housing. "There's not a one-size-fits-all solution to housing, and we know that there are a lot of people who are unable to be successful in market housing and that's where supportive housing really provides a bridge for people who may otherwise fall through the cracks and end up unhoused, " Donahue said. "In some instances, it might be a short-term stay there, but in a lot of cases it could be their forever home. " Donahue added she is proud of the work CMHA does and said while it is complex and sometimes controversial, they are onboard with community partners and trying to work to with others to be part of the solution. Stevens told the mayor and council that, now that Roots on First has been fully operational for over a year, they have had the opportunity to reflect on practices, build on its successes and address operational gaps as they emerge. "Our focus has been on strengthening accountability while maintaining a safe, low-barrier environment for those who need our services, " Stevens said, adding they have also recently increased management presence across all shifts and implemented several operational improvements, including enhanced security safety checks at every entry into the building, increased camera coverage, and more consistent monitoring practices. According to Stevens, these changes have influenced how the shelter is used, with consistent security protocols and clear expectations helping to ensure the shelter serves those who are genuinely seeking emergency accommodation and support. "While we can't control where people choose to spend the night, we can control how our shelter operates and the standards we uphold, " she said. Additionally, staff practices have been strengthened through improved documentation, situational awareness, and consistent application of shelter expectations and loss of service protocols allowing them to identify concerns early, respond proactively and promote fairness and accountability for everybody accessing its services. "An important part of this process has been reinforcing our mandate, " Stevens said. "The shelter exists to provide emergency accommodation, harm reduction supports and connection to community resources for individuals experiencing homelessness. " Stevens reiterated that homelessness, however, should not be equated with criminality, and it is important to recognize that progress is often not linear for everyone who stays with them. "Our commitment remains to operate a safe, well-managed shelter that supports some of our community's most vulnerable residents while being a responsible community partner. " Mitchell said since opening the 38-bed, year-round, low-barrier shelter for adults 19-plus, Roots on First has provided 10, 099 bed nights to 162 individuals in the community, with 30-days being the average length of stay. "People do not need to be ready for recovery before they deserve safety, shelter and human connection, " Mitchell said, adding staff also help individuals overcome barriers related to social determinants of health, including income assistance identification, health care, transportation and housing applications, which is often the first essential step towards stability. This work is supported through community partnerships, including Interior Health and B. C. 's Ministry of Social Development and Poverty Reduction, providing people with further connection to supports and services. "Progress is not always immediate but every step forward matters and stability is often what makes further changes possible, " Mitchell said. He added the supervised consumption services exist for one purpose - to keep people alive. Mayor and council respond Following the presentation mayor and council asked questions and shared further comments in a discussion that carried for more than 60-minutes. Coun. Scott Nelson remained critical of the activity and behaviour that occurs outside Roots On First, describing it as a "chaotic war zone" with many residents and businesses expressing ongoing concerns of garbage, human waste and drug paraphernalia. He pressed Donahue, Stevens and Mitchell on what they do with the core group of individuals who are prohibited from the shelter and cause issues in the community. Donahue said it is a complex problem they don't have an answer to, but would love to be part of the solution, and said individuals are only restricted from their services for their safety. Well-being and community safety coordinator Silvia Dubray said they have met with all of the RCMP Watch Commanders, establishing relationships and communications and are working hard to further strengthen them, which has helped Roots on First in numerous ways. In the past there had been some individuals staying at the shelter for criminal purposes, such as drug trafficking, according to Dubray. Stevens confirmed no one is permanently prohibited and that suspensions for repeated serious violence towards staff or clients are at the most 90-days after which a new application can be made. Donahue said while there is a broad continuum of housing, there are gaps. She believes supportive housing will fill a big piece and that the potential expansion of programs like Jubilee House, in addition to pre and post treatment care would fill even a larger piece. "I would love to see some transitional beds in this community for individuals who are trying to make change because it's a big deficit, " Donahue added. Coun. Michael Moses thanked Donahue, Stevens, and Mitchell for the update and said, as Mayor Surinderpal Rathor had noted, council is not always aware of the services and programs provided by CMHA, and that such updates are integral for them to share further information with the public and provide support. "Repeat offenders need a whole different kind of help, and where the changes are needed isn't with the shelter but the court system that's failing the community, " he added. Coun. Jazmyn Lyons said she believes housing is not the only answer and that better access to health care services is necessary. Mayor and council were unanimous in that there will be a lot of work ahead to advocate for the issue at this year's Union of BC Municipalities Convention in September.

A Toronto man sentenced Tuesday for his involvement in a 36-million cross-border cocaine and meth operation told Windsor, Ont. , court he needed to get arrested as a way out of the criminal activity. The CBC's Jason Viau reports. Toronto man in 36M cross-border drug operation sentenced in Windsor to 16 years in prison A Toronto man sentenced on Tuesday for his involvement in a 36-million cross-border cocaine and meth operation told Windsor, Ont. , court he needed to get arrested as a way out of the criminal activity. Superior Court Justice Paul Howard sentenced Marvin Watson to 16 years in prison, which was a joint submission by the Crown and defence. He's set to spend about 14 years and five months behind bars after deducting time served, crowded jail conditions and strict bail rules. The 32-year-old expressed remorse while speaking briefly to the judge. "I don't want anybody to think I'm just some money-hungry guy. I just got myself in a situation and thought the best way to get out was to get arrested, " said Watson, who didn't have a prior criminal record. Marvin Watson walks into Ontario Superior Court in Windsor to be sentenced on Tuesday. A judge gave the Toronto man a 16-year prison term for his role in a cross-border drug operation. (Jason ViauCBC) His lawyer, Frank Retar, said in court that the activity started during the COVID-19 pandemic, when Watson had a hard time finding work. In September, Watson pleaded guilty to: Importing meth and cocaine. Two counts of possession of meth for the purpose of trafficking. Laundering proceeds of crime. Possessing property obtained by a crime. In January, Howard allowed the sentencing to be delayed until July because Watson was about to become a first-time dad. The woman carrying his child, Maria Kiguru, was also part of the criminal drug ring. She pleaded guilty on Sept. 6 to laundering proceeds of crime and was given a conditional sentence of two years. CBSA found meth at Windsor-Michigan bridge It all started in March 2023 when Canada Border Services Agency officers found 300 kg of meth inside a semi-truck at the Ambassador Bridge between Windsor and Detroit. RCMP began an investigation and later found 120 kg of cocaine inside a van they said Watson was driving. More drugs were found at a residence. "There's no fentanyl. There's no heroin. There's no guns or weapons of any kind, " Retar said in court on Tuesday. The RCMP and CBSA seized 36 million worth of meth and cocaine as a part of a cross-border drug trafficking investigation. (RCMP) Both sides also agreed that Watson was more than a courier in the drug operation, but less than a mastermind. Retar shed some light in court on how Watson got started in the drug industry, pointing to difficult employment opportunities amid the COVID-19 pandemic. Retar said his client "innocently enough" began in the "marijuana distribution business. " Loads of cannabis would come from California and would be pressed in Watson's home, Retar said. 'Arrested or what's the other alternative' At one point, there was a theft, and Retar said Watson became "indebted" to the person who was giving him direction. Eventually, the operation evolved in Watson handling harder drugs, such as cocaine and meth. "He was stuck, " said Retar. "Arrested or what's the other alternative. "It's a sad commentary when an accused has to say I had to get arrested so I would be able to continue and hopefully be released from custody and live my life with my family. "

TORONTO, Sept. 16, 2025 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- The Alcohol and Gaming Commission of Ontario (AGCO) announced today that it has issued a Notice of Proposal (NOP) to suspend the liquor licence of Just Your Average Joes Sports Bar in Windsor, Ontario, for 60 days. The suspension is a result of the establishment's alleged service of a patron that contributed to a fatal motor vehicle collision last year. The AGCO is taking this action following a criminal investigation conducted by Windsor Police Service and an exchange of information with police. It was established that shortly after 11 p. m. on September 7, 2024, Windsor police officers responded to a motor vehicle collision after a motorcycle was struck by another vehicle at the intersection of Lauzon Parkway and Lauzon Line, only 500 meters from the bar. Both the motorcycle's 39-year-old driver and a 35-year-old passenger were taken to hospital with serious injuries, where the driver was later pronounced deceased. The driver of the other vehicle was arrested and transported to police headquarters. Police indicated that he showed obvious signs of intoxication and failed a breath test, and was subsequently charged with impaired operation of a conveyance causing death and impaired operation of a conveyance causing bodily harm. The AGCO's inspection has concluded that the driver had consumed at least ten alcoholic beverages at the bar before leaving. Under the Liquor Licence and Control Act, 2019 licensees in Ontario are responsible for preventing customers from being intoxicated within their premises and for ensuring their staff are properly trained to recognize signs of intoxication. Quote "Restaurants and bars that serve alcohol have a responsibility to patrons and the wider community to help prevent tragic incidents such as this one. It's both a moral and a legal obligation to operate responsibly and prevent customers from becoming intoxicated in their establishments. " - Dr. Karin Schnarr, Chief Executive Officer and Registrar, AGCO Additional information Contrary to the Liquor Licence and Control Act, 2019, Regulation 74621, subsection 43(1), the licensee permitted intoxication to occur on the licensed premises or in adjacent areas under the exclusive control of the licensee. An establishment served with a Notice of Proposal has the right to appeal the Registrar's action within 15 days to the Licence Appeal Tribunal (LAT), an adjudicative tribunal independent of the AGCO and part of Tribunals Ontario.
