Quatre individus accusés d'avoir tué un homme dans le cadre d'un violent règlement de comptes à Saint-Ignace-de-Stanbridge en décembre 2023 ont plaidé coupables à différents chefs d'accusation, jeudi dernier, au palais de justice de Sherbrooke. La victime, Jeffrey Poulin, 31 ans, était décédée de ses blessures à l'hôpital, quelques jours après l'agression sauvage. Le 23 décembre 2023, à deux jours de Noël, les quatre accusés, Jason Mercier-McGlashan, Mathieu Marceau, Philippe Fournier-Brunelle et Guillaume Marois, étaient entrés par effraction au domicile de la victime, en pleine nuit. Mercier-McGlashan et Marceau ont sorti la victime de son sommeil et l'ont ligotée avec des attaches de type Ty-Rap avant de le tabasser à coups de bâton de baseball, pendant que Fournier-Brunelle et Marois volaient drogue et argent dans la résidence. Deux des accusés, Jason Mercier-McGlashan, d'Alma, et Mathieu Marceau, de Saint-Dominique, ont plaidé coupables à des chefs d'homicide involontaire. Ils ont respectivement écopé de peines d'un peu moins de 11 ans et de 9 ans d'emprisonnement. Philippe Fournier-Brunelle et Guillaume Marois, tous deux de Granby, ont pour leur part plaidé coupables à des chefs réduits d'introduction par effraction et de vol qualifié, écopant respectivement de peines de 7 ans et demi et de 6 ans de prison. Questionnée à savoir pourquoi ces individus n'avaient jamais été accusés de meurtre dans le cadre de cette attaque violente, la procureure aux poursuites criminelles et pénales Émilie Baril-Côté explique que les policiers, avant le récent plaidoyer de culpabilité, n'avaient jamais été en mesure de déterminer qui avait porté les coups de bâton. Les policiers ont fait un très bon travail d'enquête, mais malgré ça, on n'était pas capable de savoir qui utilisait les armes amenées à l'intérieur de la résidence, a affirmé Me Baril-Côté, qui est aussi procureure en chef adjointe au bureau du DPCP de Sherbrooke On savait qu'on avait quatre individus qui avaient pénétré dans la résidence, mais à savoir lequel ou lesquels des quatre avait asséné les coups à M. Poulin, pour nous, ça ne faisait pas partie de la preuve qui était disponible, a-t-elle ajouté. Les peines d'emprisonnement pour les récidivistes violents sont au cœur du débat public ces jours-ci, alors qu'Ottawa a annoncé tout récemment son intention de modifier la réglementation pour permettre des peines plus sévères. Tous avaient des antécédents judiciaires dans ce dossier, McGlashan ayant le parcours le plus lourd. Les peines imposées sont-elles suffisantes pour donner confiance au public à l'égard du système de justice? J'espère que oui, estime la procureure. La cour s'est basée sur une décision récente de la Cour d'appel où on répertoriait 26 décisions de crimes en semblable matière. Basée là-dessus et sur les antécédents judiciaires des accusés, la cour en est venue à la conclusion que les peines suggérées étaient suffisantes dans les circonstances, conclut-elle.

Nova Scotia's Chief Medical Officer of Health Dr. Robert Strang has announced he will retire in December. I imagine he is quite exhausted. A shorthand description of the field of Public Health is that it is devoted to preventing the spread of disease and improving health through various governmental policies and societal nudges. The most famous example is perhaps its origin story, when in 1854 the physician John Snow determined that a cholera outbreak in London was related to a contaminated well and pump on Broad Street. Capping the pump corresponded with ending the outbreak. After that, Public Health embraced inoculations and a wide variety of diseases were either curtailed or, as in the case of smallpox, eliminated completely. There are a wide variety of other Public Health strategies: addressing lung cancer by encouraging people to quit smoking, reducing type 2 diabetes by trying to implement policies that reduce obesity, looking at maternal health care, examining the functioning of hospital systems, and so on. While this is important and worthy work, there has always been blowback from civil libertarians, some of whom see any governmental intervention as a threat to individual rights. We saw that in spades during the COVID lockdowns. It was perhaps inevitable that in the current hyper-politicized world and right-wing extremism, the Public Health officials trying to limit the spread of COVID would become targets. The vilification of Dr. Anthony Fauci in the United States was matched here in Canada by attacks against the then-federal Officer of Public Health, Theresa Tam, and here in Nova Scotia against Strang, who found his house picketed by COVID deniers. All of this was grossly unfair. Still, just as climate scientists before them, I think Public Health in general failed to grasp the forces working against their work and failed to rise to the occasion politically. It goes against the training and instinct of scientists to become politicized, but in both cases, bad actors had politicized their work from the start. Climate scientists and Public Health officials ignored that politicization to their own peril. And of course, Public Health officials are human, and so they're going to make mistakes. Even before COVID, Strang was oddly antagonistic to even acknowledging that Lyme disease existed, which was an unfortunate position for the Officer of Public Health at Ground Zero of the explosion of tick-related diseases to take. As well, Strang was adamantly anti-cannabis. For sure, one can take a medical position that using cannabis is bad for one's health, but Strang completely ignored social effects of criminalizing weed, which brings the full weight of racist policing and courts onto entire communities. As I get into below, the attacks on Indigenous dispensaries, which Strang endorsed, is rooted in a government monopoly on sales of alcohol and cannabis that cannot be divorced from the racist history of policing. Strang made mistakes through the COVID lockdowns. Much of that can be forgiven or at least explained by the quickly shifting scientific understanding of the disease. There are entire libraries to be written about immunologists' initial refusal to understand that COVID was primarily transmitted through the air, but that's a subject for another day. Strang's biggest mistake, in my view, was to abandon the successful policies that for the first year of the disease kept Nova Scotia as something of a mostly COVID-free oasis. As well, even now the best approach to limiting the spread of COVID and a host of other respiratory diseases is to improve indoor air quality, especially in schools and hospitals, but Public Health is not pushing the government to move on that front. But for all his faults, Strang wasn't much removed from the Public Health consensus nationally and internationally. In his personal life, he seems like a decent bloke. In the end, he was a flawed man in a necessary but imperfect field, just as a global pandemic that killed millions was politicized by bad actors. (Send this item: right click and copy this link) The province's racist monopoly on alcohol and cannabis Credit: Anne Bousquet Yesterday, the province announced it is doubling down on its crackdown on Indigenous cannabis sales: Higher fines and new offences are now in effect as part of the government's ongoing efforts to protect Nova Scotians and support a safe, regulated cannabis market. "Nova Scotia's approach to cannabis regulation is squarely focused on public health and safety, especially for our youth, " said Scott Armstrong, Attorney General and Minister of Justice. "These changes reinforce that buying and selling cannabis outside the legal market is against the law. They will help protect young people while supporting the safe, legal market for adults who choose to use cannabis. " In Nova Scotia, cannabis can be purchased legally only through the Nova Scotia Liquor Corp. (NSLC). The higher fines and new offences are intended to discourage illegal sales. Examples of increased fines include: a range of 250 to 500 for a person under 19 who possesses cannabis 600 to 5, 000 for purchasing cannabis anywhere other than the NSLC 5, 000 to 25, 000 for an individual selling cannabis illegally 15, 000 to 50, 000 for a business selling cannabis illegally. It is now an offence for illegal cannabis sellers to advertise or promote cannabis sales and for landlords to allow cannabis sales on their property. Those offences carry a fine of 25, 000. There is also a new fine for illegal sales of at least one kilogram of cannabis - twice the amount of tax that would have been paid on the legal sale. This fine works out to 3, 680 per kilogram. The fines and offences are among changes to the Cannabis Control Act passed during the spring legislature sitting and proclaimed today, June 25. The legislation is supported by new regulations. There were many conceivable ways to legalize andor decriminalize cannabis, ranging from complete deregulation to regulated dispensaries (as in Colorado) to government monopoly control of sales. Nova Scotia has chosen the latter. The province simply added cannabis to the product mix of the Nova Scotia Liquor Commission (NSLC), although unlike with alcohol, there is no provision for the sale of cannabis in private retail settings. We need to understand the history of the NSLC to understand the current cannabis situation. As I explored in "Blind Pig, " Part 2 of my "Policing Panic" series, the NSLC was created as part of grand bargain: Conservative Premier Edgar Nelson Rhodes worked to end prohibition. In part he recognized that prohibition was a failure on its own terms, but additionally, he saw the need for increasing provincial revenues to fund old age pensions, and a provincial monopoly on legal booze sales was just the opportunity. And so Rhodes forced through a plebiscite on the question of ending prohibition, which passed on Oct. 31, 1929, just a week after the Black Thursday stock market crash that ushered in the Depression. In the wake of the plebiscite, the legislature passed the Nova Scotia Liquor Control Act, but the act was loaded with provisions intended to placate the anti-booze preachers and their supporters. The Nova Scotia Liquor Control Act overturned the Nova Scotia Temperance Act, and so Nova Scotia was no longer "dry. " But the emphasis was on the "control" part of the title - the province would have a monopoly on all booze sales through the newly created Nova Scotia Liquor Corporation (NSLC), and private sales in restaurants, hotels, or taverns would have to be the subject of another municipal plebiscite, which didn't happen in Halifax until after the Second World War. And "controlling" meant policing. Previously in Nova Scotia, Halifax, Sydney, Truro, and a handful of towns had their own municipal police forces. As a rule, well into the 1920s and later, the municipal police forces in Nova Scotia were unarmed in the British fashion. In Halifax, officers could arm themselves at their own expense, but it was not a requirement. This was a contributing cause to the bumbled police pursuit in 1924 of a thief named Lew Bevis; Bevis had evaded officers in a chase leading from the Arm Bridge to Camp Hill Cemetery, where he shot and killed 28-year-old Constable Charles R. Fulton. After that, Halifax Police began issuing officers service revolvers, but the practice remained controversial. Besides the municipal forces, starting in 1920, the RCMP had a presence in Nova Scotia, but only to enforce federal law. Through the 1920s much of this work consisted of searching for Communists among the labour unions in the coal fields and, especially towards the end of the decade, rounding up anarchists and Communists for deportation. Rooting out so-called "subversives" was an overtly political act, which as we'll see in the next article in this series, had deep ramifications. Additionally, the federal Customs Preventive Service patrolled the seas and ports for rum runners and bootleggers. But rural areas had no permanent police presence. In response to a complaint made to the court, the local magistrate could order the sheriff to have someone arrested, but there were no rural police as we know them today. That changed in 1930. The provisions of the Liquor Control Act would be enforced through a newly created provincial police force, which would have a presence across all of Nova Scotia, including rural areas. The primary role of the force would be liquor enforcement, but it would also be charged with enforcing the entirety of the criminal code, and of the Highway Act. The first NSLC stores opened on Aug. 18, 1930, which was also the first day of operation for the newly created Nova Scotia Police: The first person arrested by the new force was Andrew Carter, a Black man who lived on Grafton Street, charged with "having received liquor from some person other than the Nova Scotia Liquor Commission. ". . . And just as the first person arrested by the Nova Scotia Police was a Black man, so too was the first person killed by them. The police killing of Prior James, an old man who lived near Kentville, was understood at the time as an act of racism. Here's what the Halifax Chronicle had to say about it: DEAD - HOW? The first life has been snuffed out under the new liquor law. A lonely negro has been killed. A revolver bullet pierced his heart. He fell in the misty night when darkness lends wings to terror. Press reports describe him as an inoffensive soul, harmlessly demented. He believed that a flood was coming upon the earth and had built a Noah's ark beside his door in which he might escape. He lived alone in a rude shack his own hands had built. In many homes in Nova Scotia for generations they have made a blueberry, choke-cherry, and rhubarb wine. This man had thirteen bottles of home-brew in his "ark. " The thirteen bottles cost him his life. The story reported runs that in the night a raid was made on the partially demented man's shanty. Admittance was demanded. Instead the negro fired a shot blindly through the door panel. The police then withdrew and later placed a cordon about the place. Reports say that only one officer was in full uniform. They placed two cars so that their lights shone upon the only door. Between three and four in the morning the demented man emerged. Then a running battle ensued in which it is said some thirty shots were fired. . . . So the man lies dead, dead over thirteen bottles of home-brew. . . . A life for thirteen bottles of home-made wine brings a man up with a jerk. Is it worth it? . . . Policemen not in uniform should not be tolerated making raids in the dead of night or at any other time. Firearms should not be lightly drawn. This sounds not terribly unlike many police killings today. The point is that liquor control was and is necessarily wound up with classism and racism. Daniel Sampson's mugshots, Dec. 14, 1933. Credit: Libraries and Archives Canada The Nova Scotia Police existed just three years before it was absorbed into the RCMP. One of the RCMP's first major cases in Nova Scotia resulted in the police murder of another Black man, Daniel Sampson, who was framed by police for a murder that never happened. Police fabricated a 'confession, ' lied under oath on the stand, and watched happily as Sampson was executed in the jail yard behind the courthouse on Spring Garden Road. " We can draw a direct line from the police murder of Daniel Sampson to the continued over-policing of the Black community and excessive police stops. Donald Marshall Junior was an Indigenous man who was likewise wrongfully convicted of murder due to racism. The Marshall Inquiry report later found that that miscarriage of justice was due to racism being deeply embedded in the police and justice systems. With cannabis, the policing is mostly aimed at Indigenous people. Along the way, Premier Tim Houston flat-out lied about Indigenous dispensaries. Reported Sis'moqon for the CBC: "I've talked to people in law enforcement who have told me that in this province that they've taken illegal cannabis from unregulated illegal dispensaries and tested it and found that it was laced with traces of fentanyl, " Houston said in a news conference last Thursday. "Sometimes I hear, 'I don't buy from the government supply because I don't get the same buzz. ' Well, that's probably why. " Nova Scotia RCMP contradicted that statement. "Based on the information currently available to us, the Nova Scotia RCMP is not aware of any fentanyl having been detected in cannabis products seized by the RCMP from illegal storefronts in the province, " said the RCMP in an email to CBC Indigenous. In an email to CBC Indigenous, Houston's office said the premier was speaking based on personal conversations and said he received this information from a front line police officer. The premier's office defence - that some cop said some racist bullshit and Houston was happy to repeat it as justification for policy - should offend anyone's understanding of good governance. In December, Houston's justice minister, Scott Armstrong, "directed" police agencies to crack down on Indigenous cannabis dispensaries. This political interference with policing was called out by retired law prof Wayne MacKay, reported Lyndsey Armstrong (no relation) for the Canadian Press: Wayne MacKay, professor emeritus of law at Dalhousie University in Halifax, said the justice minister has the authority to issue directives to police regarding administrative and operating procedures. But he said Armstrong's decision to order a crackdown on illegal cannabis operations appears to go too far. "The political branch of government, including the minister of justice, are not to interfere with the discretion of the police at the specific operational level in relation to either who they are pursuing or what particular laws they're enforcing, " MacKay said in an interview Thursday. MacKay compared the move to recent developments in the United States, where President Donald Trump has escalated the use of levers of presidential power to target his political rivals and pressure the Justice Department to pursue investigations and prosecutions of those he disdains. "It would be completely contrary to police independence. . . if the government was targeting specific operations to be investigated and prosecuted, " MacKay said. "That's the kind of thing, frankly, that we see happening south of the border with U. S. President Donald Trump. " As I commented at the time: Let's not pretend there isn't a backdrop of racism involved here. Along with the news release announcing Armstrong's directive, he additionally sent a letter to the 13 Mi'kmaw chiefs asking for their cooperation in the crackdown. Clearly, Armstrong's primary concern is the dispensaries located in First Nations. We could direct police attention a lot of places. Were it up to me, I'd start with the corruption and violation of workers' rights conducted in corporate boardrooms, but one could make all sorts of arguments about the allocation of limited police resources - cracking down on speeders, or intimate partner violence, or name your issue. Armstrong, however, is using his office to prioritize supposedly illegal cannabis sales in (primarily) Indigenous communities. Then Houston rolled out Strang to justify the raids on Indigenous dipensaries. "Cannabis sold outside the regulated system can have serious health impacts, " said Strang in a press release. "This is about more than enforcing laws; it's about safeguarding health and the future of our communities, and especially youth. Stronger enforcement sends a clear message that we will not allow unregulated cannabis to put Nova Scotians at risk. " Won't someone think of the children? Seriously, let's think of the children. Specifically those children who continue to grow up in a racist society that will criminalize them for any excuse, and doubly so for the excuse of maintaining a state monopoly on highly profitable alcohol and cannabis. I can't claim to have the perfect end solution for cannabis sales and regulation, but neither is it up to me. It should be arrived at through deescalation, through discussion and agreement with affected people, and with the honest acknowledgement that policing and the provincial monopoly is inextricably bound to racism. TORONTO - Lawyers for a Toronto police constable accused of leaking information to criminals in a corruption case that has rocked law enforcement in the region are asking the court to reconsider the decision to deny him bail. Const. Timothy Barnhardt is one of eight active and retired Toronto police officers charged last month in an organized crime and corruption investigation led by York Regional Police. Officials have said the probe uncovered allegations of bribery, conspiracy to commit murder and drug trafficking, among other offences. Barnhardt, 56, faces 17 charges, the most of any of the officers accused in the investigation. They include charges related to cocaine trafficking, bribery and weapons. The evidence and arguments made at the bail hearing and today's review proceedings are covered by a standard publication ban. Police investigators allege Barnhardt gave personal information to Brian Da Costa, a man suspected of several drug trafficking and bribery offences. Da Costa, one of several suspects alleged to have sought confidential information from officers, is considered a "key figure" in a criminal network that includes international ties, investigators said. His bail review hearing has not yet been scheduled. In addition to Da Costa, 18 other suspects were arrested in the investigation, including two youths. Other Toronto police officers charged include Derek McCormick, Elias Mouawad, John Madeley Jr. and his father, retired constable John Madeley Sr. , as well as Robert Black, Saurabjit Bedi and Carl Grellette. When the charges were announced last month, Toronto police Chief Myron Demkiw said the case shook the "very foundation" of public trust in the force. The accused officers have been suspended and the chief said he would seek to have some of them suspended without pay, in line with policing laws. Demkiw said officials have also asked the province's policing inspector general to conduct an independent investigation. This report by The Canadian Press was first published March 26, 2026.
